subsubtopic: COURT DECISION ON NATIVE PEOPLE'S RIGHTS IN RELATION TO JAMES BAY POWER PROJECT-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise pursuant to Standing Order 43 to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity relating to the delightful decision rendered today by the Quebec Superior Court in the injunction proceedings with respect to the James Bay project. I thought that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) would have been the first on his feet on this matter. In any event, I should like to move,
seconded by the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth):
This House looks upon the Quebec Superior Court decision in the proceedings relating to the James Bay project as being a landmark in the fight to recognize and respect aboriginal rights of the native people both in Quebec and the rest of Canada from which there must be no retreat and urges upon the government of Canada the necessity of now taking immediate and deliberative action to advance the interests of the native peoples in the James Bay area.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of importance relating to the transportation, handling and care of large numbers of animals and pets by airlines every year. Having regard to the many abuses to which these animals are exposed and the high mortality rate, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Portage (Mr. Masniuk):
That the matter of animals and pets in transit be referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications with a specific order to investigate the lack of adequate facilities at our airports for these animals.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43,1 request the unanimous consent of the House to discuss a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the present energy crisis and the fact that following a special study of the situation, American specialists have advised the American government to return to Daylight Saving Time to save their energy resources as much as possible, and that a bill aimed at saving thousands of oil and fuel barrels will be introduced before Congress shortly, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard):
That the Canadian government discuss the possibility of developing or implementing within a month some regulations or a bill aimed at using Daylight Saving Time throughout the year.

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION BY CANADIAN CONTINGENT IN MIDDLE EAST PEACEKEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House makes it possible for hon. members to examine the projected employment of Canadian troops in the area of the Arab-Israeli war. It also gives us a chance to assess Canadian participation in other

November 15, 1973
Middle East Peacekeeping Force peacekeeping operations in which Canadians have been and are taking part, so that we may learn and benefit from these past and present experiences, and thus make sure our troops are used in the most effective manner.
First of all, I believe that the proposal to send Canadian troops to the Middle East to take part in this present operation is a sound one, and that the experiences we have gained by taking part in other such operations will make it possible for our troops to do a good job in this important assignment. I and other members of the House have just recently returned from a visit to Cyprus where the Canadian delegation enroute to the NATO conference at Ankara were able to inspect the peacekeeping operations being carried out on that island. I think all of us who were there, and who had a chance to look over these operations, were very much impressed by the way our personnel in that force are carrying out their duties. I think we were all very proud to be associated with them.
I also formed the very definite opinion that Colonel Beattie, the deputy-commander of the United Nations operations in Cyprus, has a very great knowledge of what is needed to carry out a peacekeeping operation. He has been to Egypt several times to give advice on peacekeeping operations, and I think he is fully qualified to be in charge of this operation carried out by Canada.
The kind of operation which is being carried out at the present time in the area of the Arab-Israeli war, like the one in Cyprus, is that of keeping two combatants apart after a ceasefire has been arranged following bitter fighting. Important though this kind of work is, I believe, and I think we would all agree, that it is not nearly as important as keeping potential combatants from beginning hostilities in the first place. In order that we may study how we might be able to do more of this kind of important work in the future, I suggest we take a look at the operation which has been going on for a number of years to see whether improvements can be made.
As we all know, 25 years ago 14 nations of the western world joined together in a collective security pact known as NATO, which is by far the largest and most important peacekeeping operation the world has ever known. Each country pledged forces in keeping with their population and national income. Canada's contribution was a combined air and armoured unit comprised of 10,000 men. This was our contribution toward keeping the world free from devastation by a third world war. The purpose of this alliance was to convince the members of the Warsaw Pact that aggressive action would be more costly than rewarding. Largely because of the nuclear capability of the United States, a major conflict has been avoided so far.
However, at the recently concluded NATO conference in Ankara two very disturbing facts were brought to light. The first was that at the present rate of progress the Russians are expected to equal the United States capability in producing nuclear weapons in from two to three years. This projected standoff in nuclear armament will, of course, increase the importance of the conventional weapons being used by the two opposing forces in Europe.
The second bit of knowledge that came to light was that the capability of the conventional weapons used by the communist forces is being improved at a considerably faster pace than that of the weapons being used by NATO

forces. Outstanding examples of this are the SAM missiles, which are unequalled by anything on the NATO side. The second example is the Russian T 62 tank, which is the standard equipment of the communist armoured forces, and is unequalled in performance by anything except the West German Leopard, a tank which has very great speed, manoeuverability, and rate of fire. This tank can move at a rate of speed of 45 miles per hour, it is very manoeuverable and can fire at full speed. It has a rate of fire somewhat similar to that of a machine gun. It is a really remarkable piece of mechanism.
When talking with delegates from other NATO countries at this conference, and with the Secretary General, it became obvious that the Russians have used the Arab-Israeli war as a testing ground for their new weapons in exactly the same manner as the Russians and Germans used the Spanish civil war to test their new weapons in the 1930's. I think it is a well-known fact today that if the Arab fighting men and generalship had been even close or equal to that of the Israelis, with the superior equipment supplied to the Arabs by the Russians, they would have been able to win a quick victory, within two or three days at the most. In light of these facts I think we should take a look at our own country's performance in NATO forces.
Five years ago, the Canadian government unilaterally cut the strength of our contribution in half. Since then the government has allowed our tanks, which are used by our armoured force, to become worn out and obsolete. I visited the force last spring. I saw our equipment. The men who operate the equipment are absolutely first class. The equipment they have, to use, especially the tanks, is worn out, obsolete and literally held together by baling wire simply because they cannot get spare parts. It is obvious that the Russian T 62 tanks would destroy our tanks in very short order, with the obvious disastrous effects this would bring about and the high and unnecessary loss of Canadian lives.
It is obvious also that if our allies had followed the example of Canada in carrying out their NATO obligations, the greatly weakened NATO force would a long time ago have invited the Russians to engage, in some other area, in the kind of action which they promoted against Israel, and probably on a far larger scale. If there is any doubt in our minds concerning the intentions of the Russians these days, let us not forget how they moved their tanks into Hungary and Czechoslovakia. Such action undoubtedly would involve Canada and the rest of the world in a third world war.
In case there are any members in the House who have any misconceptions about the attitude of the Russians toward us, and if any of us think their attitude has softened toward the west and that they want peacefully to co-exist with us in a world of order and progress, I would ask members to listen for a few minutes to what Dr. J. M. Luns, the Secretary General of NATO, a man whose job it is to be in close touch with communist attitudes and actions, had to say at the recent NATO conference at Ankara about the situation brought about by the Arab-Israeli war. Dr. Luns said the following:
November 15, 1973

Statesmen had been speaking of a movement from a period of confrontation to a period of negotiation. There was an increasing tendency to refer to detente, not as something which we were hoping and working to bring about, but as something which was already with us; or if not actually with us, only just around the corner.
But Soviet behaviour when war broke out once more in the Middle East, raised all over again the old doubts and uncertainties about Soviet intentions, and about the genuineness of Soviet interest in a policy of detente.
I am reminded of the situation at the time that Soviet forces invaded Czechoslovakia. That, too, came as a shock at a time when East/West relations were showing signs of improvement. It seems a long time ago now. But, in fact, it was only five years. In our wishing and our hoping for a more secure and stable and peaceful world, how quickly we put aside and forget disappointments and shocking events! How ready we are to believe that things have changed for the better! Psychologists tell us that we are all inclined to remember what is agreeable and to forget what is disagreeable. This seems to go for nations as much as for individuals.
It was this behaviour, this fuelling and stoking of the flames of war, which caused us such deep concern; which provoked people into asking whether improved East/West relations could survive or had any meaning. Since then there have been some encouraging signs. There have been Dr. Kissinger's discussions with Mr. Brezhnev which led to agreement on the text of a ceasefire resolution.
Nevertheless you may well argue that the Soviet response was unduly slow in coming; that there may have been in it a certain opportunism in the light of events on the battlefield, and one could maintain that Soviet behaviour lends force to the argument that for the Soviet leadership detente is a tactic and no more. Those who hold this view argue that the purpose of detente, in Soviet eyes, is to provide the time and means needed for the Soviet Union to solve its immediate internal problems and remedy its weaknesses, for example in the management of the economy, in agriculture, in the field of technology. And once this is done, the Soviet leadership will set out once again, from a position of yet greater strength, on an old course aimed at widening Soviet influence and domination throughout the world but especially throughout Western Europe.
Mr. Speaker, those words of Dr. Luns outline the situation which exists in Europe which has been very much sharpened and brought to light by Soviet activity in promoting and supplying the Arab forces in this latest conflict. This analysis was made by a man of tremendous intelligence and respect in Europe, a man whose job it is to analyze communist intentions very accurately indeed. That is the situation in Europe which was described to those of us who were delegates to the latest NATO conference at Ankara by our fellow delegates from the other countries of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. This is the opinion of men from countries whose borders join the Warsaw Pact countries who daily can see the armed might of the communist forces across their frontier and watch them grow steadily in numbers and in combat ability.
So, in conclusion, I think it is obvious that if this country is to play its full part in by far the most important peacekeeping operation in the world today we must not forget this point. We talk very proudly of the peacekeeping operations in which we are involved, but we must not forget this operation, by far the most important, in which we are engaged today and which is aimed at preventing the beginning of a third world war. If we are to play our full part in this important operation we must immediately do two things. First, we must restore our NATO force to the numbers which we as a country solemnly and willing-
Middle East Peacekeeping Force ly pledged to NATO some 25 years ago, pledges that have been maintained by allies but not by us. Second, we must arm that force with the most modern armament that is available. To do less would be to do a disservice to our country, and would be an act of criminal negligence against the men that we ask to fight for us on the front line of Europe if a conflict should ever occur.
If we continue to act as we have, we will be acting in a way to invite aggressive action that, in my view and in the view of those attending the NATO conference in Ankara and I believe all thinking people in the world today, will eventually involve this country and the rest of the world in a third world war.

speakeroldname: Mr. Leonard Hopkins (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION BY CANADIAN CONTINGENT IN MIDDLE EAST PEACEKEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that in this discussion of the resolution concerning Canadian participation in the United Nations Emergency Force for the Middle East it is essential that we maintain our perspective on events. The pure tempo of events, the intensity of the conflict and the rapid escalation in the levels of confrontation experienced following the resumption of warfare in the Middle East on October 6, can destroy that perspective.
The warning signals for a potential conflict that would spill out of the Middle East into a possibly larger arena were becoming increasingly evident. It was essential that a mechanism be brought into play that could immediately diminish the developing confrontation and, at the same time, assist in halting the fighting on the battlefield. The United Nations Organization, with the Security Council, provided the required mechanism.
One does not have to be a historian to have a practical perspective on the events of this century. The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland) drew our attention to events in the Balkan states which eventually culminated in world war I. He also implied a possible parallel with the events of the past few weeks in the Middle East and the potential for a third world conflict. I share his concern and could not agree more with his theme.
Following world war I, an effort was made through the League of Nations to establish an organization through which future conflicts could be avoided. It did not prove to be successful. Why? The League of Nations foundered through lack of support of member nations in periods of crisis. It did not have any peacekeeping mechanisms within its structure, and I think these are two very important factors that should be considered when comparing the League of Nations and the United Nations.
Individual nations pursued isolationist policies in whole or in part during the unsettled history of the League of Nations. Isolationist policies have not contributed to world peace in past history. As a matter of fact, I believe that such policies contribute, either directly or indirectly, to world conflict. Negligence, in the assumption of responsibilities by member nations resulted in the effective collapse of the League of Nations. At this time I would like to quote a paragraph from "The Geneva Racket, 1920-1939" by Robert Dell which reads as follows;

November 15, 1973
Middle East Peacekeeping Force
From the first the League was inevitably dominated by England and France, and was predominantly a European institution, although ten of its thirty-one original members and seven of the thirteen States invited to accede to the covenant were European States. Of the four great powers with permanent seats on the Council three were European and, in the absence of the United States, Japan was the only power outside Europe that could be called a great power. China has the largest population of any country in the world and the population of Brazil is just about the same as those of France and Italy but a great power in the diplomatic sense of the term is a power with great military strength and this will continue to be the case so long as the world is ruled by power-politics.
I think it is important to point out at this time that Canada, as a middle power in the world, has shown leadership and therefore has made the peacekeeping purposes and the multipurposes leading to peace, as the role given to it by the United Nations, practical and workable in modern day history. I think that is something of which this parliament can well be proud.
World war II followed in wake of the collapse of the League of Nations. Between 1931 and 1936 Japan invaded Manchuria. In spite of the efforts by the League of Nations and its members, Japan rejected any efforts on the part of the League to settle the war. This, in itself, weakened the League. Then, between 1936 and the outbreak of world war II the following events took place as outlined in the Encyclopedia Britannica. After 1936:
... Hitler has denounced the Locarno pact (March 1936). A few months later Italy and Germany formed what was known as the Rome-Berlin axis, soon joined by Japan. All three were violently hostile to the League; among its members, only those which, like France, the U.S.S.R. or Czechoslovakia, were looking everywhere for possible support against German aggression continued to affirm their belief in collective security. While in Washington congress was passing the successive Neutrality acts, the majority of League members were declaring that they no longer considered themselves bound by the obligations of the covenant.
Although in this last period of its history the organs of the League continued to meet as before and performed some useful tasks, the main international problems were, as in the first period, dealt with outside Geneva. In the swift succession of crises-the Spanish civil war, Japan's invasion of China, the annexations of Austria, Czechoslovakia and Albania-reference to the League was either a mere formality or else omitted. When World War II broke out in Sept. 1939, no appeal of any sort was made to Geneva. Yet, in Dec. 1939 Finland did appeal for help against Soviet aggression, and the assembly decided to organize such help for Finland as it could, while the council declared the exclusion of the U.S.S.R. from the League.
No further meetings of the council or assembly took place during the war. Thanks to U.S. and Canadian hospitality, the economic and social work of the League was continued on a limited scale; but its political activity was at an end.
I use that quotation to demonstrate the fact that Canada, within the ambit of its power, at no time let down the League of Nations. Therefore, Canada is one nation that cannot be accused of causing the demise of the League of Nations. In our modern day, using the present instance in the Middle East as yet another example, Canada since the founding of the United Nations cannot be accused of letting down that organization at any stage in its history.
World War II followed in the wake of the collapse of the League of Nations. The toll in human lives, the human suffering and misery, the physical destruction that result-

ed could not continue to be tolerated by mankind. It was this realization that led to the creation of the United Nations. In the interval between the collapse of the League of Nations and the creation of the United Nations, mankind had learned that there was a requirement for a peacekeeping mechanism to be built into this new structure. What has been the result?
Many times the United Nations has been called upon to perform a peacekeeping or peace supervisory function of one form or another. Some critics say that these have not always been successful. How does one measure success? Previous explosive situations have either been defused or the level of resultant conflict contained. The potentials for world conflict have been nullified. This, to me, is success. As a Canadian I am proud that Canada has met its responsibilities as a member of the United Nations. This we have done by responding to the requests of the United Nations to make our contribution to peacekeeping activities.
Since 1948 Canadian military personnel have seen United Nations duty in Palestine, Kashmir, Korea, Egypt, the Congo, Cyprus, Lebanon, West Irian, Yemen, India and Pakistan, as well as similar but non-UN duty in Laos, Cambodia and of course, Viet Nam. They have acted in many roles; in combat, as observers, as peacekeepers, policemen, arbitrators, investigators, to name a few, and from time to time they have acted as the support element for international forces. Hon. members will agree that all these roles have been carried out with distinction. They have brought credit to Canada, but more importantly in the present context they have brought a depth of experience to the Canadian forces that cannot be matched.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I think hon. members will be interested in some comparisons between the eighth report of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence respecting United Nations peacekeeping and the current activities. The report was tabled in this House on June 5, 1970.
In respect to numbers of support troops in relation to active ground forces the report, in its recommendation concerning a stand-by military force, recommended that such a force could be made up in groups of 5,000-3,000 to be active ground forces and 2,000 men in transportation and logistic support. The figures we have been working with lately suggest a lower ratio of support troops, and this indicates that our contingent will have its work cut out for it.
Under its recommendation concerning Canadian policy the report says in part:
Since the demand for Canadian troops may not be as active infantry, continued emphasis should be placed on the development of transportation, communications and military movement expertise. While special instruction and information on the UN and the problems of peacekeeping would be useful for reserve forces, the sub-committee has concluded that the normal professional training and discipline of Canada's regular forces account for the effectiveness they have shown in past operations. It is our special administrative and technical skills, our linguistic capability and our peacekeeping experience which will be most called for in future peacekeeping situations.
These words would seem to have particular significance today.
Finally, with respect to that report, in the same section dealing with Canadian policy we find this paragraph:
November 15, 1973

The work of peacekeeping is not glamourous. It is costly. It is frustrating. It does not inspire gratitude. It does not directly assist narrow Canadian national interests. But is is an essential service-and one for which Canada has special qualification, because of her experience, because of her reputation for fairness, and because of her technical skills.
Those words speak for themselves.
A short extract from a recent editorial in the Ottawa Journal states the problem in a very realistic way:
There is much more to fielding a multinational force than the relatively simple part of providing so many soldiers and their arms to stand guard. The mechanics of command, control and support are specialized and complex. They demand a capability which Canada, perhaps more than any of the lesser powers, is able to provide. Since speed is of the essence, Canadian professionalism and experience might well be considered essential-at least at the start.
While all peacekeeping roles demand hard work, tolerance and understanding, those who have studied the subject usually agree that the logistics support of UN peacekeeping forces presents the most difficult and complex problems. While the scope of the problems differs with the area, it is always more difficult to operate away from home. Compound this with the problems of providing food, water, air and ground transport, communications, maintenance facilities and administration for a multinational group with greatly differing equipment, weapons, vehicles, clothing and even differing national diets, many speaking different languages and all demanding the best of support. Place this force in a hostile climate away from existing logistics systems, and away from normal base facilities, and one begins to appreciate the problem.
The Secretary General has asked Canada, along with Poland, to share in the logistic support of the UNEF. Canada specifically has been asked to provide the communications element, and may be requested to provide an airlift capability. Poland has been requested to provide engineering support and possibly medical support. Still to be determined by the United Nations is who will be requested to provide transport, movement control, supply and maintenance support.
Canada joins with Sweden, Ireland, Austria, Finland, Poland, Panama, Peru, Indonesia, Nepal, Ghana and two other nations yet to be named for the purpose of meeting, at the request of the United Nations, their responsibilities in contributing to the cessation of hostilities in the Middle East. We can do no less.

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION BY CANADIAN CONTINGENT IN MIDDLE EAST PEACEKEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no responsible Canadian could really oppose Canada's participation in UNEF at this point of time. Once again, the hopes and aspirations of many Canadians have been raised to a high level of expectation that we may perform the military role for which by temperament, modern tradition and size we are well suited. That is the role of peacekeeping.
I can remember as a teenager just entering high school in 1956, and beginning to read about and follow international politics, how proud I was as a young Canadian when our troops went off to the Middle East as part of the plan of the late Right Honourable Lester B. Pearson which he had placed before and had accepted by the United Nations. I can remember vividly the following summer
Middle East Peacekeeping Force attending a boy scout world jamboree in England and meeting young Israeli and Egyptian boy scouts who spoke glowingly of the efforts of Canadian soldiers who were playing a major role in preserving what they hoped would be a permanent peace in their part of the world. Little did I think then that this peace would be brutally shattered by the cruel events of June 1967 or of October 1973. Little did I foresee that our troops would be so unceremoniously expelled by Egypt on 24 hours notice in 1967, or that in 1973 we should have to beg for the right to participate again on a peacekeeping force and be accepted only as the quid pro quo for the involvement of Poland-a representative of the Warsaw Pact whose participation is clearly inimical to Israel.
As the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) pointed out yesterday, we on this side of the House have a particular and important role to play as members of the official opposition. While we all want to achieve a just, strong and permanent settlement in the Middle East and wish to provide every ounce of support we can for our Canadian troops who have been or will be dispatched, it is our responsibility, indeed our duty, to comment on the political activities of this government. We have an obligation to comment particularly on the means which were utilized to get us into the present peacekeeping framework, and the implications of that framework as it affects Canada's future in the international community and as it affects the delicate balance and maintenance of peace between the main protagonists in the dispute.
First, let me commend the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) for clearly setting forth yesterday the criteria that Canada seeks to apply when considering participation in a peacekeeping operation. I note that one of the criteria stipulates that "the parties to the conflict must accept the peacekeeping force and Canadian participation in it must be acceptable to all concerned." The minister went on yesterday to assure the House that Canada did not accept its present task until the Secretary General had given formal assurance that the presence of a Canadian contingent would be acceptable to all parties, and especially to Egypt since UNEF will be deployed on Egyptian territory. The minister yesterday stated further that he had confirmed the Egyptian agreement personally with the foreign minister of Egypt when he met him in Washington.
To all this I can only say that I hope he is right. The bitter memories of 1967 still loom large. We remember when General Nasser brought down the whole operation like a crumbling deck of cards, expelled our troops and closed the Gulf of Aqaba, all within 24 hours. I had occasion last December to visit Sharem-el-Sheick and some of the neighbouring areas where Canadian troops were deployed, and to see the remains of some of the large guns used to close the gulf, which are left today as grim reminders of the speed with which a peacekeeping operation can be closed down and booted out.
Are the assurances that we have from the Egyptians today any more valid or complete than those given in 1956? In practical terms, is the mandate of UNEF today any more sound than the mandate given 17 years ago? Indeed, is it legitimate for Canadians to ask whether the creation of the protective umbrella of UNEF in the Middle

November 15, 1973
Middle East Peacekeeping Force East is really worth all the trouble if, the moment it starts to rain, one of the parties makes us take it away?
Quite apart from all this, Mr. Speaker, let us look at some of the implied conditions under which we came to be part of the current UNEF force. We allowed our participation to be bargained by the Soviets like a wild card in a poker game. Having unashamedly sought out, and then been granted, the right to participate in this UNEF, we suddenly found ourselves cast in the role of an advocate of NATO and the U.S., to be traded-off against the participation of Poland representing the Warsaw Pact.
Consider the implications of that, being traded-off against Poland in the context of a peacekeeping force in the Middle East. Poland, a country that does not even have diplomatic relations with Isreal; a country that has openly supported the blatantly pro-Arab policies of the Soviet Union almost to the extent of being even more bellicose than the Soviets; a country in which a wave of anti-Semitism following the six-day war saw most Jews purged from all senior positions in government and industry, and eventually driven out of the country; a country where the human ovens of the concentration camps during the holocaust of World War II may have burned the brightest, even brighter than in Germany.
Consider the implications of Polish peacekeeping troops which may be deployed on Israeli soil. This is the country against which Canada was traded-off in UNEF. Does this allow us to continue calling ourselves neutral peacekeepers? Can we maintain the integrity of our supposedly neutral stance and our history of fairmindedness or have we been thrust into the role of advocate for one of the big power blocs, a counter balancing surrogate to satisfy the diplomatic manoeuvring of Egypt, the very country which kicked us out in 1967?
Is this the price that Canada must pay merely for saying that Israel has the right to exist behind secure and recognized boundaries, a fundamental provision of UN Resolution 242?
Mr. Speaker, we must never lose sight of the main goals of a peacekeeper in today's world. It is not to be part of a peacekeeping force within an assigned role to say who is right or wrong. Surely, the only role is to say what is right or wrong. I know that our well-trained and disciplined forces being sent to the Middle East will recognize the distinction, but I fear that the government may have allowed Canada, in the eyes of the world community, to be pushed into an advocate's role which blurs the distinction. In short, our position may have been compromised.
Of course, the Egyptians have not hesitated to thrust us into the advocate's position. One only need recall the story of Patrick Scott, the Toronto Star correspondent, who two weeks ago reported that an Egyptian government spokesman had said that Egypt would veto the inclusion of Canadian troops in UNEF because Canada was "pro-Zionist". Scott was later invited to leave Egypt and his press accreditation was revoked for "diplomatically embarrassing" the Egyptian government. But clearly there was sufficient evidence and subsequent stories in the Egyptian Gazette to substantiate the statement. Indeed, the Egyptian Gazette which rigidly echoes every nuance of Egyptian government policy, made it clear that Cairo had regarded the Canadian government as pro-Israeli. Again,

this indicates the surrogate position in which the Egyptians would have us serve in the Middle East, a position to which our government has succumbed.
Mr. Speaker, I am not as optimistic about the possible success of this UNEF force as I was in 1956. Perhaps I am older now and less idealistic. It is more likely, however, that conditions have changed. The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) spoke yesterday of the dangers of the unprecedented military build-up by the U.S.S.R. in the Middle East and he was right. Of course, Egypt is a client state of the Soviet now, more than it has ever been.
The right hon. gentleman was also right yesterday when he asserted that oil and the economic power that goes with it were what prompted, in the main, Soviet moves. Fortunately for Canada, the Secretary of State for External Affairs has been more unyielding in the face of Arab attempts to use oil to threaten Canada and its supplying of oil to the United States. The Secretary of State for External Affairs rightly said on Tuesday in this House that oil supplies to the United States would not be reduced in order to appease the Arabs.
I was also pleased to see the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) taking the same line on Tuesday, as did the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) yesterday in New York. One can only hope that their colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) might by now have got the message and abandoned his earlier position which, potentially, was an unwarranted capitulation to Arab demands. We wish the Secretary of State for External Affairs had been a little more astute when he went down to the United Nations almost two weeks ago and allowed our position in UNEF to be compromised by virtue of our trade-off with Poland.
The recent war in the Middle East has been a terrible war. Thousands of lives have been lost. Israel lost 1,800 of her citizens out of a population of just over 3 million. This was a terrible price for any small, isolated nation to pay. We hope that, either through the assistance of UNEF or through direct bilateral negotiations between the parties themselves, a just, lasting and permanent peace will come about, so that the residents of that part of the world may live the full kind of life to which they and others in the world are entitled.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Rowland) has set out very clearly the views of New Democratic Party members on the resolution we are discussing, and I entirely accept his statement. There are three or four points which I wish to underline. One is that I share with the hon. member for Selkirk the view that it would have been much better to have had this resolution passed before troops were actually committed to the operation. To ask us to approve at this stage, as the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) said in this debate yesterday, is asking us to approve a fait accompli. I do not believe this is a matter of form; it is a matter of substance.
In my view it is of the utmost importance for the health and survival of parliamentary democracy that major decisions in international affairs should be submitted to Par-
Middle East Peacekeeping Force liament for its approval before they have been decided upon by the government or, at least, before they are put into execution by the government. However, there may be circumstances in which that is impossible. Yet I cannot see any good reason why that could not have been done in the present case. The failure to do so has robbed this debate of any particular significance.
It is true that, when speaking for my party earlier, I indicated support for the proposal to send a Canadian contingent to the peacekeeping forces in the Middle East at the request of the Secretary General of the United Nations, as did spokesmen for the Conservative Party. I must say that I feel the government has taken parliamentary supremacy far too lightly in this instance and, indeed, in other instances.
The second point I want to make is this: we are approving the contribution which Canada is called upon to make, not because of any pressure from any of the great powers, least of all as the cat's paw of any particular great power. The request for Canadian participation has come from the Secretary General of the United Nations, acting in compliance with the almost unanimous resolution of the Security Council. My recollection is that the last relevant resolution dealing with the composition of the new international force was initiated by the so-called non-aligned nations of the Security Council. In these circumstances, I suggest it is ridiculous to say we are trying to please any one or other of the great powers. It would also be stupid to suggest that without the concurrence of the great powers such a force could achieve its purpose. If that concurrence involves some sort of geographic or ideological balance, that fact must be taken into account by the Secretary General. That is one of the facts of life which, indeed, have to be considered if the force is to be able to do the job hoped of it.
I do not think Canada should accept this role in any spirit of lightheartedness or vain glory. It is indeed a strenuous obligation. Although we acknowledge, as, indeed, it is widely acknowledged by people who know about these things, that Canada's experience and expertise in these fields are unrivaled, we cannot put forward any exclusive claim to participation in peacekeeping operations. I am fully satisfied, however, that in the present case the Secretary General of the United Nations, acting on behalf of the world community, is the person who has in fact requested, and indeed urged, our assistance. For this reason, I believe we cannot decline.
The last point I want to make is that it is in the essential interests of Canada that we do take part. A day or two ago I heard a sneering academic on the radio saying that Canada's self-interest should be our only guide and that Canada has no real interest in the Middle East. I entirely disagree. Canada is in a peculiar position as far as defence is concerned. We are part of the North American continent, which we share with a superpower. The likelihood of direct attack on Canada is almost nil. But we have been involved in the past and will be involved again if there is any world war. Our major interest in international affairs therefore is to maintain stability, which prevents the outbreak of any war and halts the spread of wars, if they do break out, before they escalate into world conflict.

November 15, 1973
Middle East Peacekeeping Force
There is no part of the world where the danger of a local conflict expanding into a world conflict is more apparent than in the Middle East where the great powers have confronted each other for many years and where their prestige is at stake. The answer to the Middle East conflict, as has been said in this debate and elsewhere, is negotiation between the parties, preferably under the auspices of the United Nations. Negotiations, however, are not possible without a ceasefire. They cannot take place while the conflict rages. For this reason, a ceasefire is essential to negotiations for a lasting peace.
On the other hand, a ceasefire requires the interposition of a neutral force to supervise the ceasefire. No one can guarantee that the UN force in this case will be able to maintain a ceasefire. There are innumerable difficulties, and impassioned fears have been aroused on both sides, but it is clear that without a peacekeeping force the probability of successful negotiation is virtually nil.
The contribution that Canada is asked to make along with the other participating nations is therefore a contribution to world stability and a direct contribution to the security and welfare of Canada. Even if one accepts the proposition that national self-interest is the basic motive for international policies, a proposition about which I confess some doubt, then that self-interest must be enlightened, and the enlightened self-interest of Canada dictates that we do our best to contribute to the stabilization of existing conflicts particularly one such as has arisen in the Middle East.
As far as I am concerned, I do not wish my support of Canada's participation in this peacekeeping force at the request of the United Nations to be negative, half-hearted or conditional. If the UN is seen to be indispensable, if peacekeeping forces are shown to be useful, I am willing to confess that I am enough of an idealist that I would rejoice in this. It seems to me the cynics have had their day and I do not question that they have had plenty of material to be cynical about both in connection with the UN and in connection with its peacekeeping operations. Nevertheless, it seems to me that the development of the UN and peacekeeping is essential to world survival.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre De Bane (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION BY CANADIAN CONTINGENT IN MIDDLE EAST PEACEKEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was born in that part of the world which has been torn apart by war and sufferings for the last 20 years, more precisely in Haifa, Palestinia, I am obviously even more afflicted than many of my fellow Canadians by the extremely distressing situation which prevails in that part of the world.
Today I will only reply to certain accusations made yesterday by the spokesman for the Official Opposition about the government's behaviour over the last few days. First, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) blames the government for its delay in consulting Parliament and, in other words, for suggesting that this was a fait accompli. He also blamed the government for showing untimely eagerness to participate in the UN forces and, to use his own terms, "Canada has no business begging to serve".

I think that those criticisms are obviously contradictory. How can anyone believe in our eagerness to participate when the debate during which the House is to approve a resolution on this question has been differed? On the contrary, if this debate has been postponed it is obviously because the government was not prepared to send troops at a time when it still could see uncertainty prevailing in the UN about the nature and amount of Canadian troops to be dispatched to the Near East. It is not so much the government's eagerness as the understandable haste of the Secretary General of the United Nations to send emergency forces which urged the Canadian government to reach a quick decision. It is not Canada's inacceptability but rather difficulties raised by other suggestions which have delayed by a week the dispatching of Canadian troops.
Even today we have no notion as to how many troops this task will require as it has not been completely defined yet. That is why the government should wisely wait and see exactly what Canada wants before asking for the opinion of Parliament. In a certain sense the opposite reproach could still be accepted; it could be said that the debate is somewhat premature since it is not yet known exactly what duties the Canadian contingent will have.
If discussion is still initiated in Parliament it is precisely because the government wanted to take the first opportunity, namely the sending of the Signal Corps, and surely it cannot be said that the government showed contempt for Parliament. On the contrary, it can be said that it is the lot of those who wanted to disregard the facts in their charges.
Of course, there are many precedents of government management, and I could quote several to refresh the memory of those who forgot about them. For example, in 1950, the Right Hon. Louis St-Laurent stated, as reported at page 494 of Hansard for 1950, and I quote:
The intention of the government is that if any other service should be required of this special force, which of course is not being created solely because of the Korean incident, if any police action, for instance, that has a warlike character should be required of it, elsewhere than Korea, the government of course would have to make its decision, but it would immediately call parliament, make that decision known and leave it to parliament to approve or disapprove of it.
The Hon. Howard Charles Green, who later became Secretary of State for External Affairs, asked him:
May I ask the Prime Minister whether there will be a resolution authorizing the sending of troops to Korea?
And the Prime Minister replied:
No, sir; that would be something which has never been done. The government announces to parliament what its policy is, and asks parliament for the ways and means to carry it out... If parliament does not authorize the ways and means to carry out the policy, it cannot be carried out. If parliament, on the other hand, on any motion of non-confidence, expresses its disapproval of the conduct of the government, of course the government resigns and some other group forms a government to carry out the will of the Canadian people as expressed by their representatives in parliament.
And in 1956 the first peacekeeping intervention in the Middle East took place. Parliament was not sitting at that time and it was called to discuss that matter on November 26, 1956. The order in council had already been made by the government on November 20. Prime Minister St. Laurent then restated the view expressed during the Korean
November 15, 1973

conflict and I would like to quote comments he added to explain the position of the government.

"That has always been the constitutional requirement and the constitutional practice that the government has to take the responsibility of making a decision and then put itself in the hands of parliament so that parliament may determine whether it will provide the funds to implement that decision or whether it will refuse to provide the funds and get another government to carry out the policies that parliament wants to have carried out. This has always been the position and this will always be the position so long as this party has the responsibility for public affairs in this country.
[ Translation]
I would like to refer now to the Congo, in 1960, when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was Prime Minister. In inviting Parliament to debate two draft resolutions, he referred first of all to the 1956 precedent, that I already mentioned, as recorded on page 7328 of Hansard of the same year.
Those are the two resolutions upon which action is now invited and the approval of parliament asked. The constitutional position in this regard was set forth by the former prime minister, Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, on November 20, 1956, when an order in council was passed which authorized the maintenance on active service of not more than 2,500 officers and men as part or in immediate support of the United Nations emergency forces in the Middle East.
Asserting his support since 1946 to the idea of Canada's contribution, the then Prime Minister, the right hon. member for Prince Albert, insisted on paying tribute to Canadian officers who had already gone to the Congo. This means that Parliament was discussing this matter while the decision was already under development. I quote from the former Prime Minister speech:
What have we done? What has been Canada's contribution? I simply outline it for the record without going into particulars. Following the initial request the government authorized the secondment of five Canadian officers who volunteered from the United Nations truce supervisory organization in Palestine. Three of the five are now in Leopoldville. When it was reported that there was the risk of a food shortage the government decided to provide pork and dried powdered milk to which reference has already been made. Then there was request for signals and logistic support for the United Nations Congo force. On receiving that request, Canadian and United Nations authorities consulted as to the precise needs to be met in the Congo.
On July 28 Canada authorized provision for the United Nations force in the Congo of up to 500 Canadian armed force personnel including a signals detachment numbering some 200, as well as a small Canadian headquarters detachment. Arrangements for sending the selected personnel to the Congo are going forward, and parliament is now being asked to approve the action in this regard.
It is to be noted that they already talked about logistic and signals support. The then Prime Minister did not consider that it was all about water carriers and wood hewers! Let me quote finally the conclusion that he was expecting-quite rightly, I suggest-from Parliament on such an occasion:
I trust that the house will give unanimous acceptance to the course we have followed, for it represents a major step forward to that day when, wherever difficulties may arise anywhere in the world, as I stated in March, 1945, the nations comprising the United Nations will all make available to an international force whatever is requisite to assure peace.
Middle East Peacekeeping Force
These were precedents and I might also quote that of Cyprus, in 1964, which is not different.
As regards the "precendent" of Indochina, I suggest that it would be quite ridiculous to refer to it since it was not the same thing from the point of view of authority, function, or nature; they were only observers and not regular forces; the decision taking process was quite different. As a matter of fact, when observers are sent away, the government simply informs Parliament of its decision and does not put forward any resolution. Therefore, this does not constitute a precendent. It is easy to accuse others when one does not know what he is talking about.
The second reproach of hon. member for Saint-Hyacin-the (Mr. Wagner) was to blame this government for their indecent hurry to contribute to the United Nations forces.
In the first place, how could one imagine that the government which had withdrawn its observers from Indochina, because it found their role ineffective in spite of their merits, was going to rush into another adventure? How could one believe that the minister, who reaffirmed on September 25 last at the General Assembly of the United Nations in New York that Canada hoped that from now on its contribution to peacekeeping operations would be governed by some criteria would suddenly alter his course? Finally, how can it be suggested that this government needs the stimulus of these operations to back up its foreign policy when it is explicitly based on strictly Canadian objectives since 1970?
However, Mr. Speaker, one thing should be specified: Canada did not ask to contribute to that UN force, but the Secretary General of the United Nations did. Documents are available to prove it. I tabled them myself in the House of Commons around November 2.
The invitation letter of the Secretary General is dated October 27. Indeed, the request was made on October 26, but Canada waited for the letter. The government even waited for another letter confirming that Canada was acceptable to all parties before taking a decision and announcing a debate on the resolution.
If the Secretary of State for External Affairs had to go to New York later, it was not to make sure of Canada's acceptability, as the hon. member suggested quite wrongly, but for other reasons. Canada had already been accepted. What are these reasons? First of all, the Secretary General has, for the first time since the United Nations have been created, the tremendous task of organizing an emergency force with the agreement of the Security Council. Previous forces were constituted like the first one, in 1956, by the General Assembly with the active support of some countries.
All those who feel strongly about the support of the United Nations and the action of the Secretary General in this very difficult task will surely avoid making fun of the Canadian government's assistance which is meant to help this emergency force to be in a position to work steadily. Moreover, other governments are perhaps less willing than ours to contribute to peacekeeping. Among the major powers, some seek above all to get well out of it. To a certain extent, this is what happened in New York, as the composition of the force has been reconsidered while this

November 15, 1973
Middle East Peacekeeping Force
is perhaps a matter or regional representation but without any political ground.
Who then has insisted on the urgency of sending just the same some vanguard elements? Obviously, the Secretary General since he was bent on having this emergency force prepared quickly before any resumption of hostilities due to the absence of any mediator. After all, an emergency force, as indicated by the words, is not a parade troop, they are, like the firemen that have been given as an example, a complement that is sent immediately before the fire can even start again.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to the remarks of the hon. member for Matane (Mr. De Bane) regarding the resolution under study. In fact, the hon. member knows the history of Middle East since he is one of its sons and became Canadian. He answered the comments made yesterday by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner).
Mr. Speaker, the resolution before us reads as follows:
That it is expedient that the Houses of Parliament do approve the Government's decision that Canadian Forces participate in the United Nations Emergency Force in the Middle East, and that this House do approve the same.
I think that such a resolution should have been submitted ten days ago after we had asked ourselves if we were ready to send Canadian forces to maintain peace in the Middle East. In doing so we should have recognized the existence of Parliament. We are asked to approve this decision when our troops are already on the spot. We are told: It was urgent to send our troops to the Middle East. And the hon. member just told us that the part our troops will play there is not known yet. Will they act as supervisors? Will they act as police officers? What part will they play? We do not know. Nothing would have prevented us from studying a resolution giving to the government the right to send troops to maintain peace on request by the United Nations. In those circumstances, there would have been no need for the government to ask us to approve its actions after the event. Our soldiers are already on the spot. Every day more of them are leaving for the Middle East while we are trying to decide whether or not the government should be allowed to send the troops.
Mr. Speaker, this is taking the bull not by the horns but by the tail and it goes against common sense. According to me, the government should not any more submit resolutions after the event.
I do not think that one single member here objects to Canada playing a peacekeeping role in any conflict whatsoever, not the role of motivator but that of a true peace-

maker. In such circumstances, we cannot deny approval of the resolution because the Canadian Armed Forces are participating in the emergency force to maintain peace in the Middle East. We could have discussed this 15 days ago. If we had not been asked to take part, we would not have done so and the government would have been free and would have had the authority to do so, with the approval of Parliament, and it would have sent these peacekeeping forces if the need had arisen, at the request of the United Nations.
Will peace be restored there? We do not know, but we certainly wish it. The parties are still there, with the Arabs on one side and the Jews on the other. Each one defends his own position. The Arabs have a history, traditions, they require that their rights be respected. On the other side, the Jews are in the same situation. I feel that the most serious problems have come about since the United Nations started interfering in the affairs of these countries. Before that, the two nations managed more or less to get along together at least better than now. With the years, the problem becomes greater and more complex. On one hand, we are assaulted from all sides, as Members of Parliament, by Arab or Egyptian organizations and on the other, by Israeli organizations which are urging us to take side.
Mr. Speaker, they are those who should make up their minds, try to compromise and understand one another since there are human beings involved and there is room for understanding and agreement between human beings of good will whose sole preoccupation is not the domination of others. In this respect, it is the Canadian Armed Forces or diplomatic corps which can intervene to encourage these nations" to understand one another and dialogue with one another, for there are people of good will on both sides. I should not like to see either Arabs or Israelis being trampled on. However, the other countries involved should stop fostering differences.
At the present time, oil is being used as a means to exert pressure on the nations which are in need of it. It has become an economic war. People are trying to make profits, but at what cost? At the cost of human lives. This is unacceptable and this is where I think Canada can play a significant role. It is useless to watch each side and wait for attacks.
Canada could invite both parties involved to do everything possible to try and dialogue in order to find grounds for agreement. Thus, Canada would gain the respect of all nations while giving people in the Middle East a chance to live comfortably in peace, and not in the type of bloody violence which we witnessed a few days ago.
Mr. Speaker, we shall support the action taken by the government, but we suggest that in future it give notice of its intention to the Parliament of Canada and ask for the authority to take part in peacekeeping operations, not only in the Middle East, but throughout the world.

Liberal government's policies, both diplomatic and military.
Before considering the area of defence policy, let us examine the actions of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp). Unless one believes that the summum bonum of Canadian foreign policy is to have Canadian participation in UN forces on every occasion, the minister's actions appear ill-considered. His statements trumpeting, or perhaps pleading, Canada's availability even before the decision to form a UN force had been taken belie his assertions that we were not preaching for a call. Perhaps the call which the Secretary of State for External Affairs longed for was one not from New York or the mid-east, but rather from Oslo. Unfortunately, the Cabinet no longer possesses a man with the unique abilities of the Secretary of State for External Affairs' illustrious predecessor.
The present situation reminds one of the quotation that when history repeats itself, the first time it is as heroics, the second time it is as comedy. I am sure the quotation is familiar to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). In his determination to have Canada included in the peacekeeping force the minister seems to have accepted, without any objection, the implicit Russian identification of Canada as a surrogate of the United States, a surrogate which had to be balanced by the inclusion of a Warsaw Pact country.
In past operations which began by being structured from the assumption that Canada was some sort of an American stand-in whose lack of objectivity was to be taken for granted, and who had to be balanced by another country with the opposite bias, our experiences have been highly unproductive. The truth is that Canadian troops are not American lackies; when they have participated in peacekeeping operations it has been with impartiality and judiciousness.

The truth of the matter is, I suspect, that none of our service battalions are available. They are not available because they have, like almost all of our forces, been over-committed and under-manned. They are in mobile command but are not mobile because of their having been committed to camp and base administrative support.
I suspect that, due to government penny-pinching over the years, these service units are required for static roles and it is deceit to imply that they are combat ready land forces, as claimed in "Defence 1971" or that they are highly mobile, as claimed in "Defence 1972". To support this thesis, I wish now to review the actions that brought our forces to this state.
Canadian troops are very capable peacekeepers: whatever tasks they are given they perform well. This is because they are capable, technically knowledgeable, well-trained and well-led. They carry out the very high tradition which has been established throughout two world wars plus their numerous peacekeeping roles. I am sure that as our Signal Regiment has been ordered to carry out the roles of a service battalion, it will do its very best to do so. I am particularly pleased to pay these compliments because their high performance has been achieved under the most execrable governmental leadership imaginable.
The armed forces of this country have been reduced and reduced. Their strength in troops has dwindled in ten years of Liberal government from 123,000 to 81,000. At the same time their civilian strength dropped from 43,000 to 32,000. I prepared a graph to show this diminution over the ten years of Liberal rule, and then extrapolated the graph to show what our forces will be in the future. If the ten-year trend continues, by 1990 there will be more civilians than troops in the department and three years later, in 1993, the last serviceman will be released. For what comfort the Canadian public may draw from it, the projection shows that there will still be 10,000 civilians administering the then non-existent forces.
The low esteem in which the present government holds the Department of National Defence is clearly demonstrated by the rapid changes in ministers. From September 23, 1970 to December 1, 1972, the department suffered under five different ministers-five ministers in 27 months. New math has an expression for zero, it is called a place-holder and this is what the defence portfolio has become, a place-holder.
Now, while these ministers were each spending their brief sojourn in defence, their policies were as one might expect, almost non-existent. I have searched diligently, Mr. Speaker, trying to find any coherent defence policy enunciated by any of these five hon. gentlemen. Regrettably, I found it particularly unfruitful to search in Han-

sard. Defence ministers appear to wait with great patience for Parliament to recess or adjourn before making any kind of statement. The present minister is carrying on this unworthy tradition, as witness his press release of October 10-I suppose it should be called an off-white paper.
In the press releases that the ministers use to delineate their non-policies, two promises appear to be constant over the years. First, there will be a reduction of troops and, second, new equipment will be bought with the money saved. They have always fulfilled the first promise, and always broken the second. Shortly after the minister issued his recent off-white paper, the Financial Post of October 20 summed up the current situation rather well:
The truth is, of course, that the defence spending freezes of recent years have all but wrecked Canada's aspirations to military efficiency. By scraping around, and laying off people, defence officials have somehow managed to pay their bills every year. But the capital budget has dried up to the point where Canadian troops are having to use obsolete equipment and face nightmare maintenance problems with such basic items as trucks. This made mockery of the Canadian armed forces and the men and women serving in them.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the decrease in the forces' strength is never accompanied by a proportional decrease in their commitments. The roles and tasks of the forces have become so numerous that "Defence 1972" has finally given up trying to list them in priority for units and has instead prepared a two-page graph with tasks across the top, units along the sides and you simply note how many X's there are. Indeed, one gets the impression that the roles were chosen by the public relations men to include every possible demand which Canada might make on a military establishment-each one, however, expressed in sufficiently vague terms as to confound any attempt at analysis-and that all the squares were X'd save only those where no possible connection could even be imagined.
Nowhere is there evidence that a logical progression was ever made from Canada's military priorities, through the organization of the troops required to satisfy these needs, to the equipment and training necessary. Instead there appears to be a grab-bag of vague objectives crossed with a military establishment to which the present government has given no clear direction. An air of fuzziness and even futility is the inevitable result.
Speaking of "Defence 72", I hope all hon. members have managed to skim through it; that is what it is designed for, to be skimmed through. It has 76 pictures which makes it particularly interesting for people who cannot read. The following comment by a learned military critic, who is able to read, best describes it:
The reports are excellent, but their excellence is in the most skillful avoidance of giving precise or specific information when it does not suit the intended image to do so. It is not that the reports are inaccurate in the strictest sense of the word, but that the inferences and omission of facts creates a very effective screen of the basic equipment deficiencies.
To get back to the forces, and the bad faith which they have been subjected to, perhaps a few examples by services might best illustrate my general thesis. In the sea element, euphemistically referred to as the navy everywhere else in the English-speaking world, we have the following situation: Ten years ago the seaborne complement was 60 per cent of the total navy force; now it is 50.5
November 15, 1973

per cent. From 1963-64 to 1973-74 the reduction in the shore complement was 1,000; the reduction in the seaborne complement was 4,750.
In comparing the Canadian Navy with other navies of the middle powers, one is immediately struck by the very large concentration on anti-submarine operations. Our ships have been designed almost exclusively for this role, and I do not wish for a minute to denigrate their capability in that role. However, I am somewhat concerned that new submarine launched missiles designed to bring down helicopters may, to some extent, nullify our efforts in this area. That, of course, is not the only concern that may be expressed. We have arrived at a very sophisticated and expensive anti-submarine destroyer group just when our role or priorities for the navy may well be changing. The Minister of the Environment and Fisheries (Mr. Davis) is hoping to obtain fishing and mineral rights for us to at least 200 miles out from our shores. This will occasion a tremendous need for armed patrol vessels, and a 4,500 ton DDH 280 would probably qualify as the least suitable vessel imaginable for the job. This is the situation coupled with the opinion that Canadian anti-submarine warfare capability has been overtaken by technology-new submarines can fire their missiles long before they can be found and sunk.
There is one final point which I would like to make before I leave the DDH 280. It is not easy to determine their cost. I hope to have an answer soon to my question on the order paper on that subject. I estimate that it is over $75 million, and I note that the United Kingdom commissioned a type 82 cruiser on March 31 last at an over-all cost of 27 million pounds, which is less than each of our destroyers cost.
Looking through Janes, I kept coming back to page 38 where Australia's fast transport ex-aircraft carrier is illustrated. It is of the Majestic class, the same as the ill fated Bonaventure. The Australian carrier was converted to a fast military transport in 1962 and can operate Wessex anti-submarine helicopters as well. Frankly, it seems to be an ideal ship to transport and provide a base for peacekeeping forces, which is our main role it seems to me.

I should like now to say a few words regarding the air element of the armed forces which seems to have been given the wrong plane or the wrong role rather consistently. The CF-5 is a plane much better suited for the distances involved in Europe and third world countries than for North American roles and ranges. As stated by Colin Gray the plane:
. . . has been given a range of missions of varying degrees of implausibility.
The next plane to come along was the much more expensive CF-104. The following was reported in "The Round Table" of July 1972:
CF-104 tactical aircraft are now being refitted from a strike-reconnaissance to a conventional attack role. It should be added that the CF-104 is singularly unsuited for this new role. The aircraft is very difficult to maintain in the field, it cannot carry much conventional payload and it lacks defensive capability. One hardly knows whether to start with the age of their trucks, the age of their tanks, or the fact that at present they have no anti-aircraft weapons at all. There has been a succession of short-term ministers, each cutting the strength of the forces, increasing the tasks-multitasking is the "in" phrase-and promising, always promising, capital expenditures on equipment. Now, our present minister has issued his proclamation of a new era. There is to be an increase of 7 per cent per annum for each year of the next five years. The deception, of course, is that the defence budget is divided between capital and operating costs. The ratio between capital and operating determines whether the force is avoiding obsolescence or not. To avoid obsolescence requires an annual share of the budget for capital costs that should be in the neighbourhood of 30 per cent of the budget. In fact, the last time that Canada spent over 16 per cent of the defence budget on capital expenditures was in 1963-64.
Now, with the operating expenditure usually taking 85 per cent to 90 per cent of the budget-remembering that operating costs rose by 11.2 per cent last year and that the inflation rate is now 8.2 per cent per annum-a raise of 7 per cent in the total budget means a decrease, not an increase in capital expenditures. It is simply more of the same fraud that has been perpetuated each year, first on the personnel in the forces, and second, on the Canadian people.
I support the idea of Canada doing what it can do to bring peace to the Middle East. I know that our troops, as always, will conduct their affairs in a highly competent and professional manner. I hope that my remarks today may in some small way move the government to change its ways and give these troops the support they have so richly earned.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have this opportunity, brief as it is, to get a few remarks on the record, and I am delighted as well to conclude this debate with something on the positive side. I was surprised at the negative tone of the last speech from the opposite side of the House. I think that that kind of speech does more harm, about which the hon. member was worried in his speech, than it does good. It is precisely the problem that we face. There is too much of the negative attitude.
I am anxious to get a few remarks on the record because, recently, I had the honour of being a member of the delegation which visited Cyprus and Turkey for the general assembly of NATO. It was an all party delegation. In the course of my remarks, had I more time, I would have liked to spend some time on the NATO conference and our role in NATO in a peacekeeping effort, but more appropriate to this debate is the role that our forces have been playing on the island of Cyprus in the UN contingent there. This is exactly related to the possibility of our doing something meaningful in the Middle East.
The population of Cyprus numbers about 600,000 people, about 120,000 Turkish Cypriots and about 480,000 Greek Cypriots, who are literally in armed confrontation with one another all over the island. There are enclaves where the Turks live in walled cities, separated from the Greek Cypriots by walls that were built centuries ago. Let me give you a more graphic picture. There is a green line that separates the Turks from the Greeks on this island of 600,000 people. This line goes the length of the island, and right through the city of Nicosia, where a few feet apart

armed patrols of each side face each other ready to fire. For every ten of these posts the United Nations force has one of its own, and still manages to keep the peace. Canadian forces have been there since the United Nations first undertook that job. Our contingent plays a key role and commands tremendous respect, so much so that it has been estimated, by persons involved in the work undertaken by other countries contributing to the UN force, that if the Canadian contingent had to be replaced, other countries would be required to supply several times their number simply because of the high degree of training and dedication of the members of the Canadian force.
This is an incredibly difficult job, yet it is being done. It is difficult in one respect because there is a temptation to say that, during the years the United Nations contingent has been there, there has been no progress, no hope of progress, and that it has incurred a tremendously high cost. There is the temptation to say that it is not our business to be there, that we should depart and let the parties go to it themselves. On the other hand, we must realize from the experiment in Cyprus, which is a living laboratory of peacekeeping operations, that its success can be measured in the avoidance of open war and savage conflict. In those terms we have made tremendous progress. And there is hope for the future, because it may be possible for future generations of those people, who hate each other so deeply, who have deep seated prejudices, to find a more enlightened approach to living with one another. That is our investment in Cyprus.
When the cost is mentioned, Mr. Speaker, in actual fact the cost may be zero because the forces we are contributing would have to be trained anyway. If we had them in our own country they would probably be doing something much less meaningful. Our contribution demonstrates above all that we do have a commitment to peace, and that we believe in peace. When we learn, in addition, that our forces are not only playing a leading role but command respect throughout the world, then we know we have learned our lessons in Cyprus well, and are willing to continue to learn. We rotate our contingent there every six months.
As a result, when we send a team of logistics experts to the Middle East, we know that we are really sending experts. When our forces are able to move for Cyprus to Egypt at 24 hours notice we can conclude, with some considerable pride, that no matter how hopeless the situation may seem in the Middle East, no matter how great and technical are the logistics problems, no matter how deep seated the prejudices and the hatred, and no matter how difficult external influences may make the situation, the fact is that we in Canada can demonstrate to the rest of the world, from our experience in Cyprus, that we do believe the peace can be kept there as well as in other parts of the world.
Our reputation as one of the most ably trained and dedicated peacekeeping forces in the world, is a reputation Canadians should prize. When we are explaining to the Canadian people the rationale for having armed forces at all, I cannot think of a rationale I would be more proud to place before the Canadian people than the fact that we are in this business not to make war but to prevent it. For that
November 15, 1973

reason I welcome the role we are asked to undertake, and I commend our forces for the role they are undertaking in Cyprus. I welcome the opportunity to go from there to another corner of the world where we can make our experience available. Mr. Speaker, we really are ready to go to any corner of the world to help keep the peace.

speechtext: A very active government.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
