speechtext:
Yes, very active in giving away the people's money to the corporations. That is exactly the issue, and I want to state the problem as clearly as I can.
The NDP has not taken the position that under no circumstances should grants be made to the private sector for research and development. It is normally held that where financial assistance is provided there should be some direct return if a successful commercial product results, or if other benefit occurs to the company concerned. We believe that when programs like IDAP, the Industrial Design Assistance Program, provide money to corporations, the least that could be done is to provide members of parliament with an evaluation of the progress made, on an annual basis. I do not know of any other legislature that is so systematic in keeping from its members the opportunity to pass judgment on spending programs.
The United States, for all its faults, is a governmental system. We are seeing some of those faults right now of course, but its system has left Canadian members of parliament in the dark ages. No member of the House of Representatives or member of the United States Senate would tolerate the restrictions imposed on members of parliament when they try to find out the efficacy of government spending. Members of the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate have virtually unlimited access to studies that have been done to evaluate government spending programs, whether they be programs of the kind under discussion now of providing assistance to the corporate sector or other programs. They have set up all kinds of investigative committees that enable them to conduct their own inquiries independent of the executive branch. In this country we are totally dependent on whether the government of the day deems it politically expedient to reveal such information.
Each year we are called upon to vote in the estimates hundreds of millions of dollars, in a state of total ignorance. We just do not know if the programs are working. We do not know if PAIT, IRDIA, or IDAP are providing the benefits that they are supposed to provide to the Canadian Public. Each year since I have been a member of this House, I have asked in a committee of the House of Commons for a systematic evaluation of the various programs. I asked the former minister of industry, trade and commerce, Mr. Pepin, and I have asked the present minister, but I have never received them. Last spring, I raised these questions again and the minister followed the bad example of his predecessor by not providing any information at all.

November 15, 1973
Industrial Design Assistance
I would refer hon. members to the reports of the Standing Committee of Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs particularly issues No. 9 and No. 14, respectively dated April 10, 1973, and May 8, 1973. Anyone who wants to take pride in the democratic political procedures in Canada would be ashamed of the testimony. It discloses a total attempt to obscure rather than make clear the results of those spending programs.
The question at stake is what guarantee we have that the moneys provided to IDAP, IRDIA or PAIT are used to the benefit of the public. How do we know that the companies getting the benefits had not already planned to undertake the particular research and development without government assistance? That is the crucial question, Mr. Speaker, and there are a number of ways of studying it. It has been done elsewhere but this government either does not want to do it or, having done it, does not want to reveal the results.
The problem can be put in a more concrete way. For example, if I own a company and, because of internal studies, am planning to expand a certain product during the next three years because my own studies show a growing market for it, then if I have any entrepreneurial talent I will go ahead. Now, if I were aware that the federal government would provide $1 million or $2 million or several hundred thousand dollars for research and development of that product, I would be mad if I did not take advantage of that benefit at the expense of the taxpayer. The point is that the moneys in this instance would not be spent in the way that was intended. It is intended that the money should be used as an incentive for a company to expand in a direction that it would not have done otherwise.
There are a lot of economists now who say that such government spending is a total waste precisely because competent businessmen in the private sector would have already made plans to expand in a certain direction even without financial assistance from the government, but they will obviously take advantage of this welfare assistance now provided by the state. It is that kind of study that we need. We have to be shown that there is a direct causal relationship between the federal government and businessmen in this area. The onus of proof is on the government to show that there is a specific action and not just express the pious hope that there is. If it cannot be established, then the program should be cancelled.

speechtext:
The government provides incentives for those who are interested in research, development and engineering. Not enough incentives are put into design. Most of the money spent in programs such as these goes to corporations, who happen to be the people who conduct business in this country. In some cases, corporations must contribute as well; in the present case, they contribute 50 per cent. That is, the corporations must contribute 50 per cent towards any design and construction process, and IDAP provides the other 50 per cent.
The question of secrecy disturbs many of us. I agree that there should be as much disclosure as possible. Of course, some caution must be exercised in dealings involving commercial agreements and intelligence. Certainly, we are entitled to any information which would not infringe on these areas.
The matter being discussed concerns me, inasmuch as design in this country simply is not good enough. I do not
November 15, 1973

think government or business has paid enough attention to design. This becomes evident when one compares our situation with that of countries of comparable economic size, such as the Scandinavian countries. The Scandinavian countries have always been very conscious of design. Their designs have always been imaginative. I have seen their products and have not seen anything superior to the way they design and manufacture various products.
Also, good design helps those countries to sell. I have had some experience in this regard, having dealt with the National Design Council in the private sector and seen the work which can be done with rather limited resources to encourage industry to think more in terms of good design. Good design involves basically engineering and better manufacturing methods. I had one experience in this regard many years ago when I was sales manager of a plastics manufacturing company.
A man came to me with a magic lantern. I had not seen one since I was a little boy. It was made of tin. I was fascinated by it. This thing was selling for around $4 at that time; then you could still get something for $4. I took it back to my office and examined it. The man wanted to duplicate it in the conventional material being used at that time, which was polystyrene. I took it to another designer friend of mine, who felt he could do many things with the lantern. The result was a product which was exceptionally well designed and which could be manufactured for much less cost than the original products. Sufficient research had been done into the material which was to be used, in this case one of the phenols, known as Bakelite. The lantern sold very well-I am going back 20 years-and sold in large volumes around the world. It could be manufactured for less than half the price of the old tin product. It was of much better design, much more functional, much less expensive and of much higher quality. That shows what you can do with good design.
Canadian manufacturers do not give design sufficient priority. We are prone to copy. Perhaps that is the difference between the Scandinavians and ourselves. We tend to go to the United States and do our design by shopping at Macy's, so to speak. In other words, a manufacturer goes down to the States, picks up a variety of things, and produces them in Canada. This is regrettable because that does not develop our export markets. I agree with the hon. member; our private sector should be developing designs. We should be doing everything in our power to encourage this.
I think that the alphabet soup programs to which the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby referred offer great opportunities for developing industry in this country. They can lead to good design and innovation. The government of Canada is responsible for many such programs. During the life of the last Parliament we tried to put these programs together in one package. The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce was responsible for many of them; other departments were responsible for others. The department developed what is known as the businessman's guide to government. Several thousand copies were circulated across this country. When business associations want to meet, they sometimes ask for copies of the publication. It is a pity that more people do not know about it. It refers to good government programs.

speechtext:
-and recall what it has done in order that we may better estimate the need for any improvement.
This program has received an enthusiastic response since its inception. It evolved in response to requests from

industry, and the primary object is to improve the competitive position of Canadian secondary industry and to expand sales in foreign markets by upgrading the design quality of Canadian products. The second objective of the program is to create in Canada an environment which will attract and retain skilled industrial design talent, initiate new Canadian designs and develop product ideas. IDAP provides assistance on a cost shared basis in support of 50 per cent of the approved cost of a design product, excluding capital costs. Projects cover the design of such diverse items as an X-ray unit, a tea kettle, a relocatable school, an automatic skate sharpener, a tent trailer and office furniture.
The first comprehensive report and evaluation of the program covers the period from its inauguration on August 17, 1970, to March 31, 1973. Over this period, 64 projects were approved for support involving an estimated total cost of $2.87 million. The IDAP commitment amounts to $1,439 million, of which $885,000 was actually paid out. The program was recommended by the National Design Council and developed by the office of design in consultation with others in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The IDAP program received treasury board approval on December 18,	1969. Departmental news
releases about the program were issued on February 17 and August 17, 1970.
The first application under the program was received by the department on August 20, 1970, and the first meeting of the IDAP Advisory Committee was held on December 17, 1970. The specific aims of the program are to improve the design quality of Canadian products and to create an economic environment in Canada which will advance the level of industrial design capability in the nation.
Projects approved for support conform to the program's selection criteria and are the subject of a formal agreement between the department and the company which ensures that if the project is successful exploitation of the results will be pursued and will contribute in an optimum way toward achievement of the objectives I have mentioned.
Assistance under the program is available to companies incorporated in Canada, to groups of companies organized as consortia, and to trade associations to the extent that they can satisfy the requirements of the program. The fundamental requirements for IDAP support are that a new or improved product will result from the IDAP project, that the project carries with it good prospects for profitable follow-on production and sales from a Canadian manufacturing base, and that the applicant company is prepared to make a substantial contribution to the development cost. The department's contribution to a project is normally 50 per cent of the approved cost.
The program's project selection criteria require objective appraisal of the merits of the development proposal and of the capabilities of the applicant company. Development proposals are appraised for innovation and for technical feasibility within time and cost constraints. The commercial aspects are appraised with respect to the needs, characteristics and size of the market, the growth of the market, tariff and non-tariff barriers to market access,
November 15, 1973

the nature of competition in the market and realistic market penetration. The capabilities of applicant companies are evaluated as to organization, facilities for follow-on exploitation and financial resources. With regard to organization, the technical, marketing and management capabilities and the corporate characteristics are of special interest.
Title to patents, designs, technical data and materials resulting from a project vests in, and remains the property of, the applicants. However, applicants must undertake not to transfer technical data or inventions, methods or processes resulting from the project to anyone for the purpose of producing or manufacturing outside Canada products identical to, or substantially the same as, the products resulting from the project without the consent of the minister. In addition to these general requirements, the following specific requirements must be met by every IDAP application. Financial support by IDAP is limited to projects concerned with the design of durable products- not throw-aways-which are produced in quantity by industrial processes and which have significant sensitivity to the physical and psychological needs of the user.
The following is a guide to the types of projects that are eligible for support by IDAP. They include office, institutional and home furniture; medical and scientific instruments; recreational and industrial vehicles; toys, games, sports equipments; craft items which are functional, such as dinnerware, ashtrays, etc.; farm and industrial machinery and implements; boats and marine products; functional clothing for sports and industry, such as fire protection suits, life jackets, etc.; household appliances and data processing and communications equipment.
IDAP does not support the design of items which are materials, such as upholstery fabrics, wall-panelling, hardwood flooring, etc.; items generally identified as components, such as gears, axles, relays, casters, etc.; items generally associated with engineering, such as submersible pumps, distribution transformers, etc.; items generally associated with architecture, such as girders, buildings, structural assemblies, etc.; items predominantly graphic, such as record-jackets, point-of-purchase packaging, books, etc.; fashion items, such as clothing, costume jewellery, etc.; or individual traditional handcrafted items of a decorative, non-functional nature such as paintings, sculptures, etc.
The product or products to be designed must be innovative. This is defined for IDAP as the practical implementation of industrial design to provide new or improved products, offering a significant advancement in form and/or function, from the user's point of view. Because design innovation is relative, its significance must be evaluated with respect to the design of similar products currently in development or already available on the market. Projects which propose design innovations based only on cost reduction or ease of manufacture are not eligible, although these factors have important additive value. Projects related to annual model changeovers, without substantial design innovation, are not eligible.
The costs for industrial designer services, whether supplied by staff or consultant designers, must be not less than 25 per cent of the total eligible costs for the project. An IDAP project must be an expansion of the design
Industrial Design Assistance
program of the company or companies making the application. The design expansion may be measured in either of two ways: as an increase in the applicant's normal budget affecting industrial design manpower, or as an expansion by the applicant into a new or highly innovative product area. Thus, an applicant company planning little or no expansion in industrial design manpower can qualify if it proposes to enter into manufacture of a totally new product line, or if it proposes to develop an exceptionally innovative product in an existing product line.
The industrial design services required for an IDAP project must be directed by a person qualified in the field of industrial design who is included in the record of designers maintained by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, or who has the qualifications that would permit his registration in the record of designers. To qualify for work on an IDAP project, an industrial designer must either have graduated in a course of industrial design from an accredited university and have had not less than two years' practical and applicable industrial design experience, which experience must be documented in a professional portfolio covering products which have actually been designed and marketed, or he must have graduated from an accredited university in a related design discipline, such as architecture or engineering, and have had not less than two years' practical and applicable industrial design experience.
This experience must have been sufficient to provide an ability to solve the types of problems normally encountered in industrial design and which relate to environmental and human factors, the integration of aesthetics with function and form, a knowledge of materials and manufacturing processes for a wide variety of markets; and this experience must be documented. Or in lieu of formal design training at the university level, an industrial designer must have had substantial practical and applicable industrial design experience of not less than five years which will have been sufficient to provide an ability to solve the types of problems normally encountered in industrial design, as I have enumerated.
Up to March 31, 1973, 64 projects had been approved. Up to that same date, 33 projects had been completed. In the year 1970-71, 11 projects were approved for a total IDAP commitment of some $226,000. In the year 1971-72, 27 projects were approved for a total commitment of $629,000; and in the year 1972-73, 26 projects were approved for a total commitment of $571,000 in that fiscal year.
One measure of the success of the IDAP program is the increase in industrial design expertise in Canada and the participation of that discipline in the program. An industrial designer was used for the first time by the applicant company in the great majority of the approved projects. Indications are that many of these companies will continue to utilize this new-found technology, and already there are proposals in hand for companies who want to obtain a second IDAP grant. Some industrial design houses have been particularly skilful in promoting the value of the program and have used it to good advantage. While most design houses have been involved in only one project to date, others have managed as many as eight.
The largest grant to date is $55,300, the smallest is $4,000, and the average grant to date is about $22,000. Allowable

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with due deference to the Chair, I do not see how we can make an assessment on whether we should have what is called for in the motion unless we have an appreciation of what is already in existence. We have here a government program, and in order to assess its efficacy we should have access to the evaluation study. Industrial Design Assistance

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to continue some of the remarks I was making last Tuesday evening at ten o'clock when the adjournment debate was called. As an hon. member has said in this debate, the bill which we are discussing is a negative piece of legislation. It accomplishes three things: it gives Ottawa, by means of a screening agency, the right to restrict the influx of foreign capital to establish a new industry; it gives the same agency the power to restrict the use of foreign capital already in Canada; and it restricts the foreign takeover of an already existing industry.
This government has once again failed to get to the root of the problem. It has submitted a piece of ad hoc legislation. It has failed to come up with a positive long-term policy to encourage Canadian participation in new and existing industries. Until such time as we can encourage large-scale Canadian investment, we will require foreign capital, and a great deal of it, unless we are content to stand still and mark time.
What kind of long-term policy should we have? In this respect I can do no better than quote from the statement made by Mr. Darcy McKeough, parliamentary assistant to the Premier of Ontario, when he appeared before the Standing Committee of Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs on Tuesday, June 19, 1973. He said:
The government of Canada must approach foreign investment positively. Its actions must be co-ordinated with and supported by federal action in tariffs, trade, taxation, competition, energy and resources policy. Each of these actions should be strongly directed toward Canadian industrial development needs, recognizing not only our basic economic goals of employment and income growth, but also the kind of lifestyle we as Canadians seek to achieve.
He also stated, and here I am paraphrasing, that Canadians should be more prominent on boards of directors of subsidiary firms in Canada; there should be increased Canadian equity participation in all Canadian-based enterprises; we should encourage portfolio rather than equity investment, and clear guidelines should be applied to the performance of foreign industry and unions in Canada.
I agree with these statements in their entirety. I believe that the present bill, because of its uncertainty and negative approach, has driven away or delayed the investment
November 15, 1973

of foreign capital in certain areas following its introduction in this House.
I was interested to read an article which appeared in the October 8 issue of the Financial Times of Canada, at page 11, about a new recycling plant being built by MacMillan Bloedel in the Oakland, California, area. It will be owned 15 per cent by the workers employed there. Under the plan, and I will not go into in detail, not only do the employees become shareholders but the corporation is provided with capital that is paid off with pre-tax dollars. Of course, United States tax laws are different from ours.
I would suggest that we must examine our tax laws and perhaps redraft them in such a manner that they will encourage Canadian corporations to utilize such a scheme and allow the workers to receive a portion of the profits. Schemes such as these, and tax laws which will allow tax credits to individuals who purchase shares in certain designated corporations, will go a long way toward substituting Canadian ownership for foreign ownership.
It is up to the government to develop a positive policy and present it to parliament as expeditiously as possible. Until such time as it does, we can only look forward to a continued feeling of foreign domination and further regional disparity.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: The hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) asked to be recognized. I recognize the hon. member.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I sincerely thank the hon. member who was ready to speak on Bill C-132 and the related amendments. I thank you for recognizing me at this time.
Bill C-132 deals with foreign investment in Canada, a question which has for a number of years interested the whole population, especially economists, whether they are partial or not to these investments. I will mention only one of them, Jacques Parizeau, from Montreal. According to him, foreign investments are not helping Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we have known for many years that our neighbours to the south have contributed significantly to the development of our natural resources, when we could have dealt with it ourselves. Today, Quebec Superior Court Justice Malouf ordered that work in the James Bay area be suspended because the provincial government has supposedly encroached upon the rights of Quebec Indians.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the James Bay development is essential, not for political reasons, but to develop-

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: To produce electricity!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
-yes, to produce electricity, but mostly to develop the province and consequently the natural resources of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, up to now the James Bay development projet has been financed by loans from the United States. I am not in agreement on this with the present Quebec premier, Mr. Bourassa. Recently, he borrowed $100 million from the United States at an interest rate of 10 per cent repayable within 25 years. This means that during that 25
Foreign Investment Review Act year-period, we will have paid $250 million in interest alone and we will still be owing the $100 million.
Mr. Speaker, when the Quebec premier came back from the United States he did not return with wheelbarrows full of American dollars. No. He came back with a promissory note under which the Quebec government undertakes to pay to American financiers $100 million bearing interest at 10 per cent for 25 years. The note is signed by Mr. Robert Bourassa and endorsed by the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, should the James Bay project not have proved profitable, Mr. Bourassa would have failed to get even two bits from the Americans. But because they saw there an electrical energy potential that might perhaps be useful to them in five or ten years from now, they said: Robert, go ahead, we are going to finance you. How? With figures we call bank credits, borrowed most of the time here in Canada, from our Canadian bankers. But to whose advantage? To the advantage of the American lenders who finance the James Bay project.
Mr. Speaker, I said and I repeated it for the last five years at least that those figures could easily have been written by the governor of the Bank of Canada, in Ottawa, if only the Quebec premier had taken the trouble to apply to that bank, which is our chief financial institution. We could thus have said: We are the owners of the James Bay development. Today, we have to say: We are the servants of some American financiers who now control 100 per cent of the James Bay development. The first contracts for building roads to that area were awarded to Americans from Cleveland and everything else is in keeping with that.
Mr. Speaker, why would Canada, the province of Quebec or some other province have to ask the American people permission to develop our natural ressources? So long as we keep on saying: Let us go get American, German, French, Spanish or Soviet capital to develop our natural resources, how can ws say that we are masters in our own house? We could so easily say it with the control of the Bank of Canadas' operations.
Even though some may think that the Creditists are dreaming in colour those who are dreaming about the United States are making even sillier dreams than the Creditists who are suggesting a logical solution to the problems currently facing us.
Bill C-132, whose purpose is to ensure our control over foreign investment in Canada, contains nothing new. We can control them without this bill. I wish to state that I am not opposed to the Americans, Germans, Hungarians or Bulgarians investing in Canada and establishing manufacturing industries or developing our resources. We are not opposed to it. However, standards should exist. We should have some regulations which would permit us to tell foreign companies: Reinvest your profits in Canada where you are doing business. Do not run away with our resources. Do not run away with the product of Canadian economic growth. Stay here to develop still further our country and provinces.
Shortly we shall be confronting our neighbours to the South about oil. The Alberta people are saying: We want to control our resources and not to be told by Ottawa what

November 15, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act we should do with the Americans. In this connection, I support the government of Alberta which says: Listen. Our natural resources belong to us. I supported premier Bennett during the discussion and fight over the Columbia River in British Columbia. This fight lasted for seven years under a Progressive Conservative Prime Minister as well as under a Liberal Prime Minister. The premier of British Columbia won his point after seven years of work.
Today, Alberta says and rightly so: We are owners of our natural resources. In the Maritime as well as the western provinces, they say: We are the owners of our fisheries. Quebec says: We are the owners of our hydroelectric resources inasmuch as we do not borrow from the Americans nor sell them these resources.
Mr. Speaker, I am far from thinking of telling the Americans to stay home, not to invest in Canada, in either Quebec or Ontario. It is important, however, that these people who are now using credit generated by our Canadian banks at least leave their profits in Canada in order to achieve the economic development of this country, to control unemployment, to fill in present economic, social and political gaps.
Mr. Speaker, the Creditists cannot work miracles and neither can Bill C-132. This legislation merely aims at letting foreigners know that they may invest here but without taking over our economy and companies, nor the operation of our natural resources. We are saying to these companies: Come to this country, but the control over our natural resources is ours, the Bank of Canada is ours. We are using it and you, from the outside, will have to abide by our laws, standards, and logical criteria in this country so that Canada remains the property of its people.
[ English]

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very anxious to put my thoughts on record on the question of foreign investment in Canada and Bill C-132, the government's answer to the problem. I say "problem," Mr. Speaker, because we have been told over and over again that there is a serious problem with respect to foreign investment in Canada.
Before I get into the matter of the bill itself I should like to dwell for a moment or two on this "problem." I feel there must be one because so many people have said so much about it for so long a time. But just what is that problem? I had hoped the government would identify it when they set out to offer a cure. Before I decide whether to accept the cure or reject it, I want to know what the problem is-and, Mr. Speaker, I do not mean that catch phrase of the NDP, "economic nationalism". As recently as last Sunday night, on CBC television the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) made another call for his version of democratic socialism in Canada.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
I am reminded that many of the countries behind the iron curtain label themselves as democratic socialists. When I hear these two words from the mouth of the leader of the NDP I worry about the implications of economic nationalism in the Canadian way of life. I cannot help feeling that if there is

a problem with respect to foreign investment in Canada, the true nature of it is quite different from what the average Canadian is led to believe.
If there is some danger that Canada is to be taken over by some group of foreigners, or if there is some danger that our Canadian identity is being threatened by outsiders, I want to know about it. I want to know just where the danger lies and I want to know the extent of the danger. I want it expressed in terms that the average citizen of our country can understand, because it is their interest that we are discussing here.
In the past, Mr. Speaker, I have heard people say that their Canadian identity was being threatened by foreign takeovers of business and industry in our country. I do not know just how this threat will materialize, but I cannot become too worried about it. I know what I am, and I am not about to let the investment of any amount of foreign capital in Alberta or Nova Scotia affect my identity. To those who complain that their identity is in any kind of jeopardy from foreign investment, I say their Canadian identity must be very fragile indeed.
My concern goes much deeper than that, Mr. Speaker, I am not concerned about the plight of the individual who is drawing a weekly salary and benefits from a firm that was established with foreign capital. I reserve my concern for the individual in this country who is not drawing salary at all and who has little or no hope of drawing one. I venture to say that the majority of the half-million unemployed in this country would not give a thought to who built the factory if they were offered a job in it. I would also suggest that those employed in the so-called foreign-owned industries would fight to keep their jobs.
One aspect of this bill which concerns me most, apart from the fact that the problem of foreign investment has not been clearly defined, is the manner in which the bill has been presented. On March 30 of this year, as recorded in Hansard the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) made the point that the federal government had not consulted the provincial governments on the question of foreign investment.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Or on anything else.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
In my view, there is no other way that a federal government could draft legislation to deal with a problem that has different implications for different regions of the country. As recorded on page 2783 of Hansard for March 30, the hon. member for Trinity said:
-it is a matter of regret to the Conservative Party that a bill of this importance to various regions of Canada should be introduced without prior consultation with the provinces.
It does not surprise me that the federal government should attempt to push legislation through this House in this manner, Mr. Speaker. I do not think anyone in this House is surprised that the government would try to push through a bill that has such far-reaching implications to the various provinces without consulting the provincial governments. It is fairly obvious that the federal government has deliberately avoided consultation and that it is not just an oversight. There must be some good reason
November 15, 1973

why the government neglected to seek the views and advice of provincial leaders in this matter. This leads me to believe that this bill is designed to satisfy the NDP economic nationalists: it is a ploy to reward the NDF for past favours and to ensure that those favours will continue for as long as the government chooses to hang on.
When I say that, I would like someone to identify the problem of foreign investment for me and to make some kind of assessment of what the probable effect is on our country. This does not indicate lack of concern, Mr. Speaker-quite the contrary. I am interested enough to want to know whether it is in fact good or bad for our country. I want to know why it is bad, as so many people have maintained, and I want to know what the alternatives are to foreign investment.
I am puzzled by the lack of hard information as to the actual effects and I am puzzled by the fact that the per capita investment in the U.S. by Canadians is greater than the per capita investment in Canada by Americans. My figures are not completely up to date, Mr. Speaker, but a year or so ago it was estimated that total U.S. investment in Canada amounted to about $50 billion. Canadian investment in the U.S. was estimated to be about half that figure, or $25 billion. This works out to a per capita investment in Canada of $161 per American. The per capita investment in the U.S. by Canadians is something like $581. There has been some talk about trying to repatriate most, if not all, of that hefty Canadian investment in U.S. securities, but in my view this is a pipe dream. There is no way that an investor can be lured away from a blue chip investment to the uncertainty of investing in Canadian industry, resources or anything else, without a great deal more security than exists today.
In fairness to ourselves and in fairness to the Canadians we are representing in this debate, if we are to recognize what the real problems are it must be recognized that Canadians invested heavily in the United States because the investment climate in that country was better. Investments which have attracted Canadian funds across the border have been secure investments which at the same time offered a good return and have not been placed in jeopardy from time to time by erratic and unreasonable tax laws. It must be admitted that whexe a person has a choice, no one is going to put his or her money in a risk venture when high yield, secure investment opportunities are offered elsewhere.
This does not mean that Canadians who invested in the U.S. and elsewhere were not good Canadians. It means, simply, that they were good business people. It means they were concerned about their investments and were not prepared to invest their savings in high-risk ventures involving resource exploration and development. Nor were they prepared to risk their capital in industry, knowing that the money market tended to be erratic and uncertain.
There is even less incentive for Canadians to invest in Canadian-based industries or ventures, Mr. Speaker. The so-called tax reforms of a year or two ago have frightened even the hardiest investors and sent many of them scurrying abroad again looking for investment opportunities. If it were so easy to get Canadians to invest in Canada, we would not be debating this bill, or at least it would be a far different bill from the one we are debating. I think it is
Foreign Investment Review Act obvious to anyone here or elsewhere that you do not just say to a person, "Be a good Canadian and invest your money in this Canadian industry or Canadian resource exploration venture." You have to talk about security of investment, you have to talk about yield, and you have to satisfy investors that their investment is not going to be eroded or wiped out by irresponsible government action.
Let us look at the other side of the coin-American investors looking for investment possibilities in Canada. First of all, it was they who took on the uncertain, high-risk ventures which opened up our north and gave impetus to our heavy industry, especially our resource industries. However, they had something going for them besides an adventuresome spirit and lots of capital. They had a government behind them which encouraged them to find minerals and to build industries to process and market them. They were allowed to keep a reasonable share for themselves-and in addition to tax incentives there were other incentives.
Let us not delude ourselves by ignoring the truths in the matter we are trying to resolve. A false premise will produce a false solution, and it is for that reason that I want to keep the government completely honest while we discuss the matter of foreign investment. Is there a real problem? If there is, what is it? Why is it a problem? Who is being adversely affected?
I believe we have to go back to the statement of the hon. member for Trinity earlier this year to find the answer to those questions, Mr. Speaker. We must go back to square one, consult the provinces and determine which, if any, of the provinces feel there is a serious problem with respect to foreign investment. I cannot accept the view that we are going to lose our identity if we do not throw a few investors out of our country. So I am not satisfied that what we are discussing is purely a federal matter which can be settled by isolating the question and excluding all of those who are really concerned, in a dollars and cents way, about the question of investment both foreign and domestic.
Nova Scotia and New Brunswick would give a far different answer to such a question than would British Columbia or Alberta. If we do not ask them, we are never likely to know for sure what they want. If domestic investment capital and domestic investors were readily available to the have-not provinces, I do not think they would care what we do about foreign investment. But we know all too well that there has not been a rush, on the part of domestic investors, to the Maritimes or to the prairies. Why should there be, Mr. Speaker, when they can find opportunities for investment in other countries where the investments are more secure and where governments are more understanding?
I was appalled at the thinking of the government when the question of foreign investment was capturing the public imagination a couple of years ago, thanks to the economic nationalists, hon. members to my left in the NDP and assorted other personal interest groups. Someone must have thought this talk would result in a great rush on the part of Canadians to buy up everything in sight and that we would suddenly find new millionaires springing

November 15, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act up overnight all over Canada. The government could not wait to introduce a capital gains tax. In my view, if Canadians had felt the urge to invest in Canada, then this move frightened most, if not all of them, out of the market.

But I am convinced that we are able to deal with foreign investors in the same way as we deal with Canadians, through existing Canadian laws. If there are loopholes, let us by all means plug them; but let us not chase will-o'-the-wisps in the name of Canadian nationalism or in any other name. Everyone in Canada, whether Canadian born, foreign born, or even a visitor, is subject to the same laws and I cannot bring myself to support new laws unless there is a demonstrated need for them. We may, in fact, need foreign investment controls and regulations, but let us not rush them into being until they have been proven to be required.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will take this opportunity of making a few comments on Bill C-132 which still is very important. I must say I have had the possibility of giving some opinions a few months ago on what is termed a legislation on foreign investment.
Having heard all the statements, it is obvious that we are looking for mechanisms or a legislation aiming at a take-over by Canadians of their industry and economy. I also feel that it is important to stress all the services that foreign investments or investors have brought into the country. I think that it is important not to reject these investments lightly. On the contrary, I think that we have the responsibility of establishing some mechanisms and to find a certain motivation for Canadians as regards the necessary investments for the expansion of our industries.
I think that this would be a much more positive way than throwing out or blaming foreigners for coming here to finance or invest in projects which are definitely interesting. Of course, foreigners do not come here simply to please Canadians. On the contrary, there is interesting business to be done in Canada, and these businessmen are always interested in greater profit. Therefore I think that we have the responsibility of attempting to motivate Canadians to invest more in our Canadian businesses.
I would also like to mention that I have already hoped for the sales promotion of our Canadian products. I think that this speaks to the pride of Canadians and that is something that many of us lack. We should think more

often about the necessity to encourage Canadian firms and their products, so that they may attain a more competitive position on world markets.
When we talk about foreign investments, we are seeking economic independence for Canada. And then, we take for granted that it is probably through very strong incentives given to Canadians eager to invest in our industry that we may acquire this economic independence. So, whether we like it or not, if we want to be independent as Canadians, we shall have to pay the price sooner or later. We must therefore adopt measures which may mean sacrifices for us, but if we are really sincere when we say that we want to put our economy back into the hands of Canadians, we must also accept a number of sacrifices.
For a number of years, we have heard of a revolution in industrial development. It would be desirable that the development and all related investments be made by Canadians. Again, there might be a lack of incentive and inducement so that Canadians would prefer foreign investors.
There is always the same question of incentive. Even though we introduce new legislation or changes in legislation, if we do not succeed in stimulating and interesting Canadians I feel we are in the wrong direction. It is clear that the foreign investor as well as the Canadian businessman will not care about investing money in a Canadian corporation. I think that in order to motivate Canadians and interest them we have to offer them some advantages. So, during the few minutes left to me, I would like to urge hon. members to think about this possibility.
It is very easy to talk about these nice principles and I think it is an example which could interest Canadians in investing more in Canadian companies. We would simply have to consider the possibility of giving a deduction of up to $500 on the dividends for every investment made by Canadians in Canadian companies. I think that the fact of having a deduction of $500 on dividends would prompt any Canadian to invest in Canadian companies. If this Canadian benefited from such an advantage it would mean that at current interest rates he would have invested about $6,000 in a company.
We are well aware of the interesting effects that it could bring to the Canadian who, being interested in a company, holding an equity and having been motivated to invest his money, would become a better citizen, a Canadian more interested in his country's affairs. Therefore, he would become much more interested in his country's businesses; it might be surprising to find out how many Canadians could invest small amounts which would build up into a sizeable fund to help the economic development of Canada.
I imagine that the minister or the appropriate department will find other proposals as interesting and efficient as my own. I think that would be a way of creating motivation for Canadians.
Once more, as I said, all that motivation and pride we must have as Canadians demands sacrifices. So, through an interest we could awaken in individuals we would manage to help considerably industry and curb foreign influence on the Canadian economy. A step such as the
November 15, 1973

one I suggest could have very interesting effects in various respects.
I would also like to take this occasion to express my views on an amendment now before the House, namely the right of veto for the provinces. Personally, I would be tempted to support that amendment since I always regarded highly the right to speak, the right to act for the provinces in co-operation with the federal government; however, I feel that considering our system we have an obligation to give the provinces the right to express themselves on foreign investment that in some cases may not have the influence hoped for but in other cases may often bring the province new possibilities. That is true but as members of this House we have a responsibility to give the provinces the right to speak, negotiate, consult, and finally the right of veto on foreign investment.
I think it is perfectly normal in the present system for the provinces to have a say in and be consulted on foreign investment.
I would also like to remind the government, on the occasion of the study of this very important bill, that the present situation related to oil is particular and must make us think twice about what may be the result on our economic future of an overly heavy influence by companies whose majority of shares are not held by Canadians.
It seems to me entirely justified to talk about the establishment of a national corporation to mitigate a little that influence which the oil companies seem to have on the government.
In my opinion, a national corporation would likely give Canada some control. I believe the present situation is a perfect illustration of the absolute power of those companies. Of course, we have every reason to ask for the creation of such a corporation which could give the government, therefore the people, some control again.
Those were the remarks I wanted to make, Mr. Speaker, because I think that as members of Parliament we have suggestions and opinions to offer. I hope the government will take them into consideration and I insist that Canadians will find a greater Canadian identity and be more interested in investing in their economy inasmuch as they will be motivated by legislation introduced in the House of Commons. Thus we will succeed in reducing the influence of foreign investors on our future.
We naturally seek a degree of economic independence in Canada and I think that making Canadians consider their future with pride, concern and responsibility and introducing very practical and interesting measures is the way to achieve the aim that every member of the House is pursuing.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise to participate in the debate on Bill C-132 I have the thought and feeling that few issues of Canadian economic policy in the past ten years have aroused as much interest, yet as little resolution, as those surrounding foreign investment and particularly the changes proposed in this bill. The approach to the problems of direct foreign investment has to date involved the development of a collection of policies in the form of laws and agreements of a unilateral, bilateral and multilateral nature. In general, this approach has been one of ad hoc reaction often associated with a particular individual who has shown an interest in the topic and the problems as they have arisen. This approach has obviously not been successful.
Other members on this side of the House have pointed out that this bill is so strongly biased against foreign investment that it would damage the Canadian economy. This is a possibility. Quite obviously, the extent to which this is true will depend largely upon the willingness and ability of Canadians to fill any void that may be created. Large new capital investments are required in Canada on a scale well in excess of previous experience. If Canadians and the Canadian government are unable to meet this

challenge, then of course our economic prospects will be affected and our present standard of living will be greatly eroded.
There are a number of small and medium sized private businesses in this country-indeed, a number of them are in my riding of Elgin. I have frequently been told that this bill places a particularly heavy burden on small businesses whose resources are already strained to the limit in reporting to the government. I share their concern. The government can go a long way toward alleviating these fears by simply issuing guidelines which would let small businesses know exactly where they stand. This government has shown it has a total lack of vision and courage in projecting even five years ahead. In fact, it would be a great feat if we could manage to get the government to think past the next crisis which we as a nation will have to face, instead of edging along day by day on this ad hoc, crisis-to-crisis basis.
On an over-all Canadian basis, some acceptable alternative to the present trend must be found. When we reach the point, as we did five years ago when over 46 per cent of our metal fabricating industry, over 86 per cent of our transportation equipment industry, over 71 per cent of our machinery industry and over 99 per cent of our petroleum and coal products industry-as measured by total assets- was owned by people outside Canada, then we reach a rather sobering situation. Since then, the level of foreign ownership has continued to increase. Something must be done, and we must reassess our position.
I believe it is extremely important that my party's position on this matter and on the amendments we have put forth should be considered very seriously. The honorable member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), the party spokesman for industry, trade and commerce, has pointed out many times that the real problems facing Canada have not been dealt with in this bill. More importantly, however, he has pointed out a sound and positive approach to help Canada in its present position. First, the Progressive Conservative Party's full employment proposals would include a more expansionary budget. Our second point is that we believe our tax laws must be changed so as to encourage greater savings, greater investment and risktaking by our fellow Canadians. At the present time, taxwise an American in many cases is in a more opportune position to invest in Canada, in many fields, than is a Canadian. This situation must be changed to ensure that a Canadian has an advantage if he or she wishes to invest in such fields in their own country. This thought is basic and any other suggestion is certainly ridiculous.
Third, we say that Canadian business in general has fallen behind the world in the last few years in research and development. Federal leadership is required to allow us to regain our momentum in this important field. We intend to outline certain proposals to allow our businesses, especially those which are Canadian-controlled, to regain their position in the world. Let me underline our party's position. Research and development are the forerunners of business development. During the past ten years Canada, with all its resources and with all its potential, has fallen into the bottom third of the world's first 25 countries in terms of rate of growth per capita. For a country with the
November 15, 1973

potential Canada has, this is an extremely sad situation. It is time this trend was changed.
Fourth, our party believes our financial institutions should be redirected and restructured to ensure that Canadian business can be properly financed within Canada, including proper financing of regional activities of companies in our five main regions. Fifth, we believe that through a more aggressive export policy, a positive trade balance in current account can be achieved exclusive of whatever resources are sold. Such a positive balance would create a cash pool which could then be directed toward acquiring substantial or controlling interest in Canadian institutions now foreign-controlled. There are many fields in which we believe Canadians could buy sufficient equity to ensure our control of many of the multinational corporations. In this regard we are suggesting it is high time Canada started to live as part of the economic world.
To summarize, most Canadians are in favour of economic nationalism. But the question is: What is economic nationalism? To some, it is the taking of positive economic steps to strengthen Canada's position at home and abroad. To others, it is the welcoming of foreign or Canadian investment and technology to achieve these ends, with proper safeguards to protect Canadian industry. To this end, greater co-operation between the provinces and the federal government is required.
Several provincial premiers have spoken out against the bill, stating that the federal government would not fully take into account the special needs, aspirations and interests of a particular province. This is a real and very dangerous problem that must be faced and resolved by consultation rather than confrontation.
In a world of economic change, where Canada has much to gain and even more to lose, it would be unfortunate if we embraced a form of negative nationalism wherein the exponents were anti-foreign and, in particular, antiAmerican. In rather emotional arguments, these negative nationalists take statistics on foreign ownership and use them out of context in an alarming way. They allege that various types of ownership are harmful, without meaningful proof. They fail to appreciate Canada's involvement in today's multinational world economy and they put forth no creditable alternatives to replace what they would destroy.
The positive Progressive Conservative policy that has been outlined many times on this subject is far more important than anything the government has offered. In fact, the only thing the government has done is to show the country that it does not understand the economic world of today. We have tried to show that it is possible not to just keep a situation from further deterioration but to do something about it and move in the direction of a real solution involving greater Canadian participation and incentives for Canadians to invest more heavily and actively in this great country-Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this very important debate on foreign ownership I wish to deal generally with the bill,
Foreign Investment Review Act and especially with some of the amendments. We in Saskatchewan view with suspicion what appears to be a desire by the federal government for more control over the provinces. We look at the DREE programs, the LIP program and some of the other programs which do not seem to be designed having us in mind.
Today such cliches as "Buy Canada back", "Canada for Canadians", and so on, are very popular. Foreign capital has been necessary in the past. It is here and we can live with it. The challenge really is how to maintain control when using foreign investment, and not how to stumble along without it. In fact, it is difficult to get Canadians to invest in high-risk ventures such as oil exploration. There seems to be a correlation between the distance from Ottawa and the confidence in the government. This might explain why people from other countries more readily invest in high-risk ventures in Canada than do Canadians. A good deal of investment capital will be required, for example, in oil exploration alone. It is estimated that $30 billion will be needed during the next ten years for exploration if we are to maintain and ensure security of supply. It is doubtful that this amount of money could be raised in Canada; therefore, we will have to look to foreign investment.
I should like to deal specifically with the amendment of the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). I believe this amendment to be of particular interest to the people of Saskatchewan who have always viewed with a great deal of suspicion the motives of eastern bankers and eastern businessmen. In a recent publication by Norman Bromberger, entitled "Conflict and co-operation", there is an outline of the problems of credit in Saskatchewan, particularly farm credit. In his opening remarks Mr. Bromberger states that the settlement and development of western Canada was promoted to develop eastern commerce and industry. Further, he makes the statement- this is following confederation-that westward expansion served the interests of two sections of Canadian business, that is, the railroad interests and the growing commercial and industrial interests. He also states that although western settlement did not come with confederation as anticipated, it was a deliberate policy decision by eastern business and commerce to set up a hinterland for commercial and industrial exploitation. So the people in western Canada-which includes Saskatchewan-have for a long time had a deep-rooted suspicion that central and eastern Canada are not out to do them much good in terms of investment.
The finding of investment capital in Saskatchewan has always been a problem. In recent years, provincial governments have been involved with new enterprises entering their provinces. I would mention examples such as the Interprovincial Steel Company and the Prince Albert Pulp Company. The premiers of all provincial governments went south to the United States, where they found the required money. Then they came back and started the businesses. In the case of Interprovincial Steel Company, I believe this has been quite a valuable acquisition for the city of Regina and the province of Saskatchewan. I am wondering whether that business would have been established under this proposed legislation.

November 15, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act for Central Nova (Mr. Mackay). It is a worthy subamendment and one with which the hon. member for Yukon would certainly agree.
The hon. member for Timiskaming said some interesting things when he moved his subamendment. There is a great deal of oil in the Yukon. Oil was discovered over 100 years ago in the Norman Wells area of the Yukon. We would like to think that the Canadian market would be made available for that oil-but that will not happen unless we have foreign capital. It will take $5 billion or $6 billion to build a gas line down the Mackenzie Valley. If the gas line is built, you will see extensive drilling taking place along the route. Of course, it would be even more costly to build an oil pipeline down the Mackenzie Valley.
Some members of the NDP have a mistaken belief that the oil in Alberta does not belong to Alberta, does not belong to Canada but belongs to somebody in a foreign country. The oil now being found and developed in the province of Alberta belongs to the people of Alberta. The oil companies don't own it; they could not extract one barrel of oil without the permission of the provincial energy board. How much they extract from each well is determined by that energy board. There is no ownership of the oil itself. There is ownership of the drilling rights; they buy the drilling rights, and pay a very steep premium for them, but it cannot be said that they own the oil in the ground. Albertans own the oil in the ground, and they limit the amount that comes out. As I was saying, there is room for great potential development in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon.
The minister's speech in support of this legislation was rather weak. In an earlier energy debate in this House the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) said that we are being strangled by private enterprise. I thought that was a rather strange statement, but perhaps coming from him it is not strange. He has got himself hired on as a two-bit professor at some university and now he has become an academic and a long-haired theorist on socialism.
At one time we sat in this House and wondered if the Waffles would take over the NDP. But they did not have to do that, Mr. Speaker; they were swallowed up. No Waffle member could say more in support of state control than the statement uttered by that hon. member, that we are being strangled by private enterprise. We need private enterprise to move into the territories and help develop their resources so that Canadians will have continuous reserves of oil and gas. There is absolutely no need for Canada to be short of oil or gas this winter. But because we have not encouraged enough money to come in and develop our resources, we may well remain at the mercy of the Middle East and its pricing system.
An editorial in the Financial Post of November 10 contained the following:
Our major expansion money is going into the U.S. Our Canadian growth will level out, while our U.S. growth will really take off.
That is a quotation from a statement made by a company president. That is certainly what will happen if this bill goes ahead. The minister piloting this legislation is from Toronto. A few wealthy Torontonians have told him there is enough money in the country to develop it-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your counsel. I always pay close attention to it and will attempt to adhere to the amendment. Apparently some hon. members are not aware of what the subamendment would do. It does not deal with the Yukon, but just says; -following the words "a province" the words "or a territorial council".
There are two territorial councils, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. Provinces are not necessarily named in the amendment. I just point that out so that next time the "Brownie" seeker jumps up he will use the right word. There is certainly great potential for gas and oil recovery in the Northwest Territories-but that is not all that is there. There is a tremendous amount of mineral wealth there, and it needs to be developed. I remember when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Die-fenbaker) was prime minister he introduced the roads to resources program. Many roads were built up to those resources so that the mining and development necessary to get the metals to market could begin. That was a very worth-while project, and it took capital which the government of the day advanced to the provinces and the territories. The roads moved the minerals out and the Pine Point railroad also moved the minerals out. However, despite what some people might think, we cannot move the oil and gas very efficiently because if any means other than a pipeline is employed, huge amounts of foreign investment
November 15, 1973

will be necessary. If we do get the pipeline down the Mackenzie Valley, this will require further foreign investment.
I read a moment ago a newspaper article which says that foreign investment will be curtailed. It says that our major expansion money is going to the U.S., that Canadian growth will level out while U.S. growth will really take off, and that this kind of loss hurts. Another headline in the same paper says that every major cost and tax will be higher in Canada. That is interesting, Mr. Speaker. We are not keeping up with our major competitor for money, the United States.
This afternoon the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) said that few people live in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, and that more people in his constituency voted for him than live up there altogether. This will continue to be the case as long as we keep out the foreign investment that is necessary to develop that area. It is all well and good for the lost souls from Saskatchewan in the New Democratic Party to say they have to manage their economy and curtail their growth. Saskatchewan is a very rich province in minerals, but it is very afraid to develop and it has frightened off foreign investment. Some of that investment has come to Alberta, where we have confidence in ourselves and in the province. We are not afraid of managing foreign money and I think we have done a relatively good job of it under the present and former governments.
The federal government could do it, too. Foreign investment could not go into the Northwest Territories without full consultation with the federal government, because that area does not yet have provincial status. I suppose the NDP would like to think they would curtail the growth there so that their power over the people living in the area would remain in Ottawa and they would never be given provincial status. I do not agree with that, Mr. Speaker. Canada is a vast country, a very regional country, a confederation of areas-and those areas should be encouraged to grow and develop.
I notice that no one in this House speaks out strongly against development in the north at James Bay. That is a similar region and huge amounts of foreign capital are going into it. Why do we say that we must control the foreign investment going into the Yukon and the Northwest Territories? Is it because they are undeveloped areas and we want to keep them undeveloped so that control will remain here; so that the population will always be small and will never bother Ottawa very much?
I should like to pose a question to the minister in charge of this bill. When he sets up his agency, will there be somebody on it from the territorial Councils, because of the rich mineral wealth that is there?

Mr. Speaker, I too am strongly in favour of strong provincial input into these matters we are discussing-and I think the territories were not included in the legislation because of an oversight. The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), moved an amendment which may

correct this glaring oversight. I am sure the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) is entirely in agreement with it.
The territories, even more than the provinces, are concerned about representation with respect to decisions affecting investments. Some suggest that as there are only a few thousand people in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, we do not really need to bother about them. Some say there are too few people up there to affect the resources of the region. I ask, what about the neighboring state of Alaska? Compared with the population of New York state, California or other states in the U.S.A., the population of Alaska is very small indeed. Yet that state is important. It is equally important for the people in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon to have a say in decisions affecting investments in their area. Why, Mr. Speaker? The reason has to do with discoveries of oil and gas and with the building of pipelines in those areas.
The courts have pointed out that jurisdiction and ownership with respect to thousands of square miles of land in the Yukon and Northwest Territories will need to be examined if we are to build pipelines from those areas. It is important for native peoples and others affected to have some input into decisions respecting investment in areas in which they live. This investment, in the foreseeable future, will take the form of gas and oil pipelines and things like that. In the previous parliament we discussed the Yukon minerals legislation. It was found that a group of civil servants in Ottawa had designed the minerals legislation for the Yukon. It was an autocratic piece of legislation which did not take into account certain needs and was detrimental to the development of the Yukon.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

TRANSPORT-PREVENTION OF ABRIDGEMENT OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND'S RIGHT TO FERRY LINK WITH MAINLAND-POSSIBILITY OF GOVERNMENT OPERATION OF SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 18 I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) if he was actively seeking means whereby P.E.I.'s constitutional right to transportation links with the rest of Canada should not again be abridged. I further inquired whether he was giving consideration to having the ferries operated by the Department of Transport. For some reason, the minister in his reply talked about the right to strike and asked whether hon. members wished to remove the right to strike. My question was not one dealing with labour relations. Rather, it was concerned with transportation and the right of Prince Edward Island
November 15, 1973

to be connected with the rest of the Dominion by reliable and adequate transportation links.
This chamber, and the one which existed before the great fire of 1916, echoed with the complaints of Prince Edward Island members of parliament troubled about their province's lack of transportation facilities. A vital question when we entered confederation a century ago was transportation. We entered because we were promised continuous and efficient communication with the mainland. This hundred-year old promise was never fully implemented. It certainly was very much in abeyance during the last railway strike and two preceding ones.
It is a strange thing that Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, the two provinces from which the CNR has made a most thorough withdrawal, should suffer most when the CNR and its employees have a row which brings on a strike. The vast number of people crossing on the Island ferries are not railway passengers at all. Yet the ferries are operated by the CNR. My belief is that that corporation should be removed from the picture and the ferries operated directly by the Department of Transport. Premier Campbell has suggested a provincial Crown corporation to operate the service. I cannot see this as a realistic notion. The province of Prince Edward Island could not afford to operate the ferry service, nor should it. Interprovincial transport is purely and simply, clearly and definitely, the responsibility of the government of the Dominion of Canada.
But what troubles me most about the whole matter is the lack of action and communication between the government of Prince Edward Island and the government of Canada on this vital link. Surely the break-off of service should have shocked both governments into action. But on October 29, in reply to an order paper question, I learned there had been no formal communication from the government of Prince Edward Island or suggestions for the avoidance of any future cessation of service on the Bord-en-Tormentine run. No formal word from the Prince Edward Island government, and from the federal department the reply, "The continuance of alternate routes should guarantee that Prince Edward Island is not completely isolated in the event of future work stoppages."
In other words we are back to where we were last summer, six years ago, and in 1951. Leave it to the Northumberland ferries! They did a good job and I am surprised they have not been paid for their great work. I am surprised, too, that the P.E.I. government has not presented a bill for what it had to do to relieve some of the strain of the shutdown of the main ferry service.
However, the status quo is not good enough and I think the minister should do something. I do not think our island province deserves to be cut off as it was three times in recent years. Now is the time to move. Now is the time to learn the lessons of the strike. Montesque said that to govern is to foresee. Let us see some foresight, some action, some concern on this vital issue.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-PREVENTION OF ABRIDGEMENT OF PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND'S RIGHT TO FERRY LINK WITH MAINLAND-POSSIBILITY OF GOVERNMENT OPERATION OF SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the fall of 1972 a team of CN and MOT officials began examining the
Adjournment Debate
organizational structures of the east coast ferry services to Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island and considering alternates. Many alternatives were considered, among which were: creating a separate entity for ferry services that would report to the CN vice-president responsible for the Atlantic region; creating a separate CN subsidiary with its own board of directors; creating a Crown corporation; bringing east coast ferry service activities into the public service.
On October 12, 1973, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) jointly announced with the president of CN a new east coast ferry operating administration to be based at Moncton, New Brunswick, with operating units in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, responsible for all ferry and coastal services managed by CN for the Ministry of Transport. Featured in the reorganization was the creation of a directing committee for the new administration, composed of senior Transport and CN officials. CN president J. MacMillan announced that Rupert J. Tingley, formerly CN area manager in Newfoundland, had been appointed as general manager. The major objectives for the new administration are the co-ordination, improvement and expansion of the present ferry and coastal services to meet expected increased traffic demands.
It should be noted that in regard to all of the alternatives employees would either have by law the right to strike or be able to choose the right to strike as a means of dispute settlement. Even if by some means the services could be declared essential and prohibited from striking, there is no guarantee that the employees under certain conditions might not find it necessary or desirable to initiate a work stoppage. One way of avoiding shutdown of the ferry services would be to have the services run by the military, but this has never been considered a viable alternative. The government is not considering abolishing the right to strike.

The Toronto Globe and Mail of this morning comments editorially:
Almost from the day Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau brought in the present abortion rules he has been under attack for not liberalizing them further. He has kept doggedly to his stand that the government would not consider further reforms so soon after the 1969 changes. The existing system works and there is no need for further relaxing the rules, he says. He's wrong. The present system works but it works badly. Therapeutic committees are cumbersome. Some hospitals will not establish committees. Others interpret the abortion section of the Criminal Code so strictly that whole communities are denied the right to abortions. Contraception is the first line of defence against unwanted pregnancy. We are far from that state of affairs today. Meanwhile we must get rid of our present abortion legislation which gives rise to such absurdity and injustice all across this country.
