subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE-REQUEST THAT ABORTION BE REMOVED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Montreal case will probably be appealed but we cannot make comments on the future development of events concerning possible amendments to the Criminal Code.
The general position of the minister inside and outside the House is as follows: He objects to any amendment to the abortion legislation as it now stands.
The hon. member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) has insisted that abortion legislation should be liberalized and amended according to the decision of the U.S. Supreme Court. It has also been stated that in several areas, hospitals refuse to set up abortion committees thus overburdening other hospitals and compelling women who wish to obtain an abortion to travel to other provinces or abroad or still to rely on those who practise illegal abortions.

On August 25, 1970, in the 10 provinces and Yukon Territory, it was reported that 143 hospitals had appointed therapeutic abortion committees. Their distribution is as follows: Newfoundland, 4; Prince Edward Island, 2; Nova Scotia, 6; New Brunswick, 7; Quebec, 16; Ontario, 48; Manitoba, 4; Saskatchewan, 8; Alberta, 18; British Columbia, 29; Yukon, 1.
It appears that the abortion rates vary considerably among the provinces and are in no way connected with the availability of chartered or approved hospitals which have appointed therapeutic abortion committees. The statistics for the first six months of 1972 are also available. The therepeutic abortion rate, compared with the total number of births, had been 7.6 per cent for the first semester of
1971.	In 1972, for the same period, the rate was 10.1 per cent. Here again the rates varied according to the provinces. For the first six months of 1971, the statistics varied from 19.3 in British Columbia to 0.5 in Newfoundland. For the same period in 1972, these rates were 22.4 in British Columbia and 1.2 in Newfoundland. For the period of January to June 1972, the total of therapeutic abortions was 18,817. For the same period in 1971, the total was 14,168.
The number of abortions for women from elsewhere or residing in the province, other than those reported in the province, was negligible. In 1971, foreign residents accounted for 0.1 per cent. During the same year, patients residing in a province other than that concerned in the report represented 0.7 per cent of the total. For the first six months of 1972, the figures are the same. AIR CANADA-CONSTRUCTION OF NEW COMPUTER CENTRE AT DORVAL-EFFECT ON WINNIPEG CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the past few months I have spoken several times on the subject of Air Canada and for the most part my remarks have concerned the transfer of the Air Canada overhaul and maintenance base to Dorval in 1969. This House is quite familiar with the circumstances surrounding that transfer and the destructive effect the move has had on the aerospace industry of Manitoba. I believe that part of the base should be returned to Winnipeg.
Tonight I intend to discuss a situation which in many ways bears an ominous resemblance to the transfer fiasco.
November 15, 1973

I refer to the construction by Air Canada of a new computer and systems service centre at Dorval. In spite of assurances to the contrary from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), I fear that this new facility might render the computer operation in Winnipeg obsolete. Such a move would force many employees to move to Dorval.
I am skeptical of the minister's assurances because they resemble those false assurances about the maintenance base given to the people of Manitoba during the 1950s and 1960s. Successive Liberal governments repeatedly denied that the base was to be moved-but it was. One thousand Manitobans were forced to move to Dorval. Today, employee morale is incredibly low, especially among transplanted Manitobans. The people of Winnipeg do not want a repeat of the air base debacle. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) termed the transfer "one of the worst mistakes ever made in Canadian history". We do not want to be the victims of another government mistake.
The new computer building is scheduled for occupancy in January. But who exactly is going to occupy the 25,000 square feet of floor space? Air Canada maintains that the building will house employees and equipment presently located in various other areas of the base. However, there appears to be some doubt whether a building of this size is necessary if in fact it is to be occupied only by those currently working in Dorval.
A letter sent last spring by Air Canada to Winnipeg's civic executive policy committee stated that the airline was moving the Winnipeg accounting department to Montreal. Air Canada, however, claimed that this information was erroneous and have since continued to assert that no facilities will be moved. But for obvious reasons I am skeptical, and so are employees at the Winnipeg branch. History has made it hard for us to be confident of government assurances.
Even with the guarantee that the computer centre will remain in Winnipeg, the Manitoba aviation industry will continue to flounder. The government has failed to live up to past commitments. I suggest that rather than moving the Winnipeg branch to Dorval, Air Canada should centralize its computer facilities in Winnipeg. It is functionally possible to locate a central computer for all Air Canada requirements outside central Canada, with no loss of efficiency. Both the TransCanada Telephone Company and CN-CP Telecommunications are technically able to provide data transmission at reasonable cost because rates are rapidly becoming distance-insensitive.
Most airlines in the United States have decentralized their operations. United Airlines has its headquarters in Chicago and its main computer in the western city of Denver. Eastern Airlines has its head offices in New York but has computer centres in North Carolina and Florida. However, according to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Guay) this is not what the government means when it speaks of decentralization. The hon. member stated in a recent letter to me that centralization "does not apply directly to such Crown corporations as Air Canada". I quote further from his letter:
Air Canada is, of course, expected, as a Crown corporation, to recognize the government's social and economic policy. However, any decision regarding the actual operation of Air Canada must be
Adjournment Debate
left to its management which is responsible for the performance of the airline.
This is without doubt one of the most incredible statements I have read since becoming a member of parliament. I suggest that as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport the hon. member should read the Air Canada Act. Crown corporations are clearly subject to the people through parliament and are dependent upon parliament, especially the cabinet, for policy orientation. To imply, as the hon. member does, that Air Canada runs its own affairs independent of the cabinet is an insult to hon. members' intelligence.
An example of just how much direct influence the cabinet does have in formulating Air Canada policy can be found in a decision by the airline last spring to extend a contract to CAE aircraft in Winnipeg. CAE was awarded a contract to build galley equipment for Air Canada's New Lockheed jets without even having entered a bid. Furthermore, CAE had no experience in this type of work. Noor-duyn Norseman Limited of Montreal had won the contract with a $200,000 bid, but was later informed by Air Canada that the contract was to be assigned to CAE.
CAE is Air Canada's replacement at the Winnipeg base and has been plagued with difficulties. Former Air Canada president, John Baldwin, frankly admitted "it will cost us more, substantially more, to have the galley equipment, and so on, built by CAE". He also said the airline had an obligation to Winnipeg. It is obvious that Air Canada was advised by the government to give the contract to CAE, yet the parliamentary secretary asserts that Air Canada makes all its own decisions. Even Mr. Baldwin admits this is not so.
Thus, the government does control Air Canada policy and is in a position to steer that corporation on a road to decentralization. This it must do. Not only must the computer office remain in Winnipeg but the government should consider centralizing all computer facilities in that city. This, combined with the return of portions of the air base, would not only alleviate the deteriorating situations in Dorval and Winnipeg but would prove to the people of Manitoba and western Canada that this government is sincere when it talks about decentralization.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to say that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) was already on the air on this subject on station CJOB yesterday morning, making the same statement as he made here a moment ago and making many allegations which he cannot substantiate. If he has a real problem, let him spell it out here, instead of all this literary writing that he is doing in the House.
In fact, Peter Ward, the investigating reporter for CJOB, said on that station recently that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre was known to exaggerate. I think that I myself would not want this said about me. Speaking about CAE, this is another thing. He should read in the House the letter which he received from the manager of CAE in Winnipeg contradicting what the hon. member said on the air, in the House and elsewhere.

November 15, 1973
Adjournment Debate
After taking this into consideration, I would now like to return to the matter of the computer. On June 6, the day after the hon. member asked his question in the House, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) sent him a letter in reply. The situation, contrary to the allegations made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and also by another member of the opposition, has not changed since then.
Air Canada is changing computer equipment at both Winnipeg and Montreal and some computer operators are regularly transferred in these operations. Those transferred from Winnipeg are replaced, and the total staff size in Winnipeg is being maintained at last year's level. Beyond this I can really only repeat the substance of the minister's June 9 letter, that Air Canada's plans are to result in a significant upgrading in technological resources at Winnipeg. Through a new, flexible terminal
computer, Winnipeg is being interlinked with Toronto and Dorval real-time computer capabilities and the technology available at both these locations is thus becoming available to the Winnipeg group. That is contrary to what the hon. member keeps saying. The Winnipeg group is having its knowledge updated accordingly.
Air Canada regards it of prime importance that the same relative levels of advanced technology be achieved, regardless of geographical location, to provide uniformly up to date and efficient service to all Air Canada users of computer services at any of their prime three locations and to ensure equal opportunity for promotion to all their employees across their system.
